oven-cooker:fan oven element.title: About the oven heating parts
oven-cooker:fan oven element.description: A fan oven that runs but doesn't heat usually points to the fan-oven element — the fan proves the oven has power, but the element is what produces the heat. This reference shows where the element and the other heating parts sit, and the safe, no-dismantle checks worth making first. Fitting a new oven element is a job for a qualified engineer.
oven-cooker:fan oven element.relatedCheck: identify the fan-oven element and the safe pre-checks for a fan oven that runs but does not heat
oven-cooker:fan oven element.alt: Reference diagram: an oven with its heating element, thermostat/temperature sensor, fan motor, thermal cut-out and door seal labelled, alongside customer-safe checks

provenance.title: WhichPart generic appliance reference diagram
provenance.basis: Identifies the fan-oven element and heating parts for a grounded oven-cooker:element (not heating) diagnosis where the customer's differential includes the fan oven element. ABOUT identification/explanation only — not a DIY repair instruction.

oven-cooker:element._approved: Oven heating-path reasoning: identify cavity/function/mode, what still works, programmer state, then the electrical path that mode uses. Fan-runs/no-heat is a strong element candidate, not a proven purchase. Cross-mode top-oven/grill is topology, not a deterministic element or selector rule.
symptoms: grill works but fan oven doesnt heat
element glowing red in one spot

components.name: which function works (fan/grill/top/base) - identify first
supports: one mode heats but another doesn't
grill works but fan oven is cold
top browns but base doesn't
against: nothing heats in any mode (=> supply/terminal-block/thermostat/thermal-cutout)

components.name: clock/timer set to AUTO (power-cut free fix)
supports: stopped after a power cut / power switched off at the wall
clock flashing / reset
display works but the oven won't heat
against: clock set correctly to MANUAL and it still won't heat

components.name: fan / rear ring element [fan-oven mode]
supports: the cooking fan is running normally but the fan oven stays cold (strong candidate, not proven)
fan-oven mode selected
a visibly split/blistered/holed ring element
against: the fan itself isn't turning (=> fan motor / obstruction)
nothing heats in any mode (=> supply/terminal-block/thermostat)
clock/programmer flashing or left in AUTO after a power interruption (set MANUAL first — not a part)

components.name: grill element [grill mode]
supports: grill alone won't glow/toast while other independent heating functions work
a visibly split/blown grill element
against: the same upper-cavity heating system heats normally in top-oven mode (series path) while grill-mode is incomplete — that argues against a simple open element and keeps the mode-specific control/supply path in play
fan oven cold but grill works (different element — fan-oven path)

components.name: base / bottom element [conventional/base mode]
supports: food pale/undercooked underneath, top browns
conventional/base mode affected, other modes fine
against: all modes cold

components.name: top element [where a separate top element is fitted]
supports: top won't brown, lower heat works, modes needing the top element affected
against: model has no separate top element (grill doubles as top)

components.name: element terminal connectors (burnt)
supports: burnt/discoloured connector at the element tags
intermittent heat
against: clean connectors and a proven open element

components.name: selector / function switch
supports: several loads fail only on particular selector positions
behaviour changes with mode on the same heating system (top-oven vs grill)
burnt selector contacts/terminals
against: a visibly open/split element with other modes switching correctly
clock/programmer still in AUTO after power loss

components.name: grill energy regulator / simmerstat
supports: grill-mode power/glow is incomplete while top-oven heating on the same system is normal
grill heat varies incorrectly with the grill control
against: a visibly open grill element
every heating function dead (=> supply/programmer)

components.name: oven thermostat (not switching on)
supports: no click when the thermostat is turned
never calls for heat
against: runs too hot / doesn't regulate (=> thermostat overheating node)

commonConfusion.name: no heat = the fan motor
commonConfusion.note: If the FAN IS TURNING, the fan motor is proven good. That does NOT automatically prove the fan/ring element has failed — wiring, selector contacts, thermostat/control and supply remain realistic. The motor is only the cause if the fan isn't turning or is noisy.
wouldApplyIf: the fan isn't turning or is noisy

commonConfusion.name: no heat = PCB
commonConfusion.note: Down-rank the PCB. For no-heat the element (which-function), selector contact, thermostat and (if dead) supply/terminal-block come first.
wouldApplyIf: element, selector, thermostat and supply all proven good

commonConfusion.name: dead after a power cut = failed part
commonConfusion.note: Control-state, not a part. After power loss many ovens leave the programmer in automatic/timed mode; heating is inhibited until MANUAL. Do not recommend a timer, PCB or element until that is ruled out.
wouldApplyIf: still won't heat once the clock is set correctly to MANUAL

discriminators: Reason cavity/function/mode first, then what still works, then programmer/control state, then the electrical/heating path that mode uses, then compare across modes. A plausible component hypothesis is not purchase grain.

FAN RUNNING + fan-oven mode + cavity COLD: the fan motor is proven good. The fan/rear RING ELEMENT is a strong diagnostic candidate, not proven. Also keep burnt wiring/connectors, selector/function/main switch, thermostat/control path, and supply. Do not turn this into an unconditional element diagnosis or a model-for-part request.

PRESERVED FUNCTION is diagnostic, not generic 'oven not heating'. Grill works / fan oven cold is a different path from grill-partly-works-in-grill-mode while the same heating system heats in top-oven mode. Do not collapse them.

TOP OVEN vs GRILL topology (two-cavity): top-oven mode can wire element sections in SERIES (~half mains, heats without glowing bright red). Grill mode switches to full mains so they can glow/toast. 'Heats in top-oven' does not prove the grill path is healthy. 'Part of the grill works' does not prove the element is the failed part. Cross-mode evidence must keep the mode-specific control/supply path (selector/function switch, grill energy regulator/simmerstat, wiring) as well as the element — without swapping 'always element' for 'always selector'.

POWER-CUT / FLASHING PROGRAMMER: oven appears dead + clock/programmer flashing + recent power interruption => the programmer is often in automatic/timed state. Return to MANUAL. This is a control-state/use-condition, NOT a parts recommendation. Do not surface parts until that has been ruled out.

Engineer check order for COMPLETE no-heat (no mode producing heat): 1) the relevant element, 2) burnt element terminal connectors, 3) the selector/main switch, 4) the oven thermostat. A function-split is not complete no-heat. PCB last. VISIBLE element damage (split, blistered, holed sheath) strongly supports that element as a hypothesis still short of automatic purchase unless the rest of the path is accounted for.
Do NOT diagnose GAS ignition unless the oven is explicitly GAS or a flame/burner/pilot is mentioned (this is the electric-oven element path).
adviceBeforeReplacement: identify cavity, which function/mode is affected, and what still works
after a power cut, or if the clock is flashing, set the clock/timer to MANUAL and the correct time before anything else
a visibly split/blistered element can be identified by eye (power off)
oven-cooker:element.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:element.clarifyingQuestion: Which cavity and function is affected (fan oven, top oven, grill, base), what still works, and is the clock or programmer flashing or left on automatic after a power cut?
oven-cooker:element.secondaryQuestion: In the affected cavity, does the same heating system behave differently in top-oven mode versus grill mode?

oven-cooker:tripping-electrics._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). RCD trips => an element leaking to earth. Timing (cold vs after heating) is evidence. CRITICAL: neutrals are commoned/linked, so the function that trips does NOT prove which element leaks. STOP repeated resets; no insulation testing.
symptoms: trips as soon as i turn it on
trips when the grill is on

components.name: heating element leaking to earth (base/grill/fan/top)
supports: trips the RCD/fuse - most often a heating element leaking to earth
the BASE element is a frequent culprit (spillage drips onto it and arcs to earth)
trips as it heats/once hot (leakage rises with temperature)
against: it goes cold WITHOUT tripping the power (=> thermostat/cutout)

components.name: element terminal connectors / wiring to earth
supports: burnt/wet connector or chafed wiring shorting to the chassis
against: clean dry wiring and a proven element leak

components.name: control / relay board (last)
supports: elements and wiring proven sound
against: a classic element earth leak not yet excluded

commonConfusion.name: trips on the grill = the grill element is faulty
commonConfusion.note: NOT proven. Neutrals and electrical paths can be shared across grill/top, fan-oven and base elements and switched through common/main switching, so a leaking element elsewhere can trip when another function is selected. Do not recommend replacing the selected function's element from the tripping symptom. Insulation/leakage diagnosis is competent-person territory.
wouldApplyIf: it trips only on a particular function - use it as evidence, not proof

commonConfusion.name: tripping = thermostat
commonConfusion.note: Tripping the RCD is an earth fault (an element), not the thermostat. Only treat it as thermostat/cutout if it goes cold WITHOUT tripping.
wouldApplyIf: it goes cold without cutting the power

discriminators: An oven that trips the RCD/fuse often has a HEATING ELEMENT leaking to earth. Insulation leakage can rise as an element heats, so 'starts then trips once hot' is useful timing evidence. It does not identify which element.

CRITICAL - SHARED ELECTRICAL PATHS: grill/top, fan-oven and base elements can share neutrals and be switched through common/main switching. The function that trips is evidence, NOT proof of which element is leaking. Do not confidently recommend replacing the selected function's element from the tripping symptom.

SAFETY: leakage diagnosis is competent-person territory. Repeated tripping (or any burning) => STOP USE. Do NOT instruct insulation-resistance / megger tests, live probing, energising exposed components, disconnecting earth, bypassing the RCD, or repeatedly resetting to reproduce the fault.
adviceBeforeReplacement: note WHEN it trips (immediately / as it heats / once hot) and on which function
don't keep resetting the RCD to reproduce it; a repeatedly tripping oven should be taken out of use
do not treat the selected function as identifying the leaking element; this needs a qualified electrician/engineer
oven-cooker:tripping-electrics.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply. Repeated RCD tripping => stop using the oven; this needs a qualified electrician/engineer, not consumer insulation testing.
oven-cooker:tripping-electrics.clarifyingQuestion: Does it actually trip the electrics/RCD (versus just going cold), and does it trip straight away or only after it's been heating for a while?
oven-cooker:tripping-electrics.secondaryQuestion: Does it trip on more than one function, and have you had spillage onto the base of the oven?

safetyInformation.text: An oven that keeps tripping your electrics, or smells of burning, may have an electrical fault. Stop using it and switch it off at the fuse box / consumer unit (ovens are often wired in, not plugged), don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician.
safetyInformation.hazard: Dangerous wiring or an insulation fault; ovens are frequently hard-wired, so isolation is at the consumer unit rather than a plug.
safetyInformation.applicability: Oven trips the electrics, or there is a burning smell / scorching.

provenance.title: Electrical items — Fire safety at home

discriminators: ONLY diagnose gas ignition when the oven is explicitly GAS, or a flame / burner / pilot / gas is mentioned. A plain electric 'no heat' with no gas cue is the ELEMENT, not ignition.

A GAS oven/burner that lights then goes out, won't stay lit, or won't heat at all (while the grill/hob still work) is most often the FLAME FAILURE DEVICE (FSD/FFD) - the safety that shuts the gas off when it doesn't sense a flame (via its thermocouple/flame probe). Check the FFD/thermocouple FIRST, then the oven ignitor/glowbar, then the gas valve.
This is a GAS fault, NOT an electric element.
oven-cooker:ignition.clarifyingQuestion: Is it a gas oven, and does the burner light at all or not even spark?

oven-cooker:fan-motor._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). CAVITY/COOKING fan: relevant when the fan is NOISY or NOT TURNING. Fan turning but no heat => fan ELEMENT, not the motor. Distinct from the cooling fan.
symptoms: horrible noise from the back of the oven when the fan runs

components.name: obstruction / fan blade fouling the rear cover
supports: scraping/ticking as the blade catches the rear cover/shroud
something fouling the blade
against: clear blade and a dead/silent fan

components.name: fan blade (loose/distorted)
supports: rattle or scraping from a loose/bent blade
blade contacting the cover
against: deep rumble from the bearing (motor)

components.name: cavity fan motor
supports: fan doesn't turn at all in fan mode
rumbling/rough bearing noise
fan slow/intermittent with the blade free
against: the fan turns fine but there's no heat (=> fan element)

components.name: fan thermal cut-out / wiring
supports: fan dead with a tripped thermal cutout or broken wiring
against: fan runs normally

commonConfusion.name: fan oven no heat = fan motor
commonConfusion.note: If the fan IS TURNING, the motor is proven fine. That does not automatically make the fan/ring ELEMENT a purchase — wiring, selector and supply remain realistic. The motor is only the cause when the fan is noisy or not turning.
wouldApplyIf: the fan is noisy or clearly not turning

commonConfusion.name: noisy fan = cooling fan
commonConfusion.note: The cavity/cooking fan (behind the rear plate, circulates heat) is different from the cooling fan (cools the controls). Match the symptom to the right fan.
wouldApplyIf: controls getting hot / cuts-out-hot => cooling fan instead

discriminators: The cavity fan MOTOR is the culprit only when the fan is NOISY (scrape/rattle/rumble) or clearly NOT TURNING. If the fan turns but there's no heat, the motor is proven good — the heating/supply path (element, connectors, selector, thermostat) is then in play; do not treat the element as an automatic purchase.

Route noise by CHARACTER: SCRAPING/TICKING => blade fouling the rear cover / distorted blade / obstruction; RUMBLING/ROUGH => fan motor bearing; RATTLE => loose blade/fixing/panel; SLOW/INTERMITTENT => fan motor (or obstruction/wiring).
Distinguish the CAVITY/cooking fan from the COOLING fan (cools the controls) - different component and symptoms.
adviceBeforeReplacement: select a fan-only programme and look through the glass to see if the cavity fan spins
establish the noise character; check for a blade fouling the rear cover or an obstruction
oven-cooker:fan-motor.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:fan-motor.clarifyingQuestion: Is the fan noisy or not spinning, or is it spinning fine but the oven just isn't heating?
oven-cooker:fan-motor.secondaryQuestion: What does the noise sound like - scraping/ticking, a deep rumble, or a rattle?

oven-cooker:thermostat._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). Temperature-incorrect / overheating / cuts-out-hot-without-trip. Architecture-aware: mechanical thermostat vs electronic temperature sensor+control. If it TRIPS the RCD => element earth leakage. If it cuts out hot and RECOVERS when cool => cooling fan/thermal cutout.
symptoms: too hot even on a low setting
heats up then goes cold then hot again
cuts out after a few minutes without tripping

components.name: mechanical oven thermostat [dial/capillary ovens]
supports: burns everything / runs too hot on a dial-thermostat oven
never cycles off
the capillary/phial or thermostat not regulating
against: an electronic/sensor-controlled oven (=> temperature sensor/control)

components.name: oven temperature sensor + control [electronic ovens]
supports: electronic-control oven running too hot/cold
temperature bears little relation to the setting
against: a simple mechanical dial thermostat

components.name: safety/overheat thermal cut-out
supports: cuts out once hot WITHOUT tripping the electrics, recovers when cool
against: it TRIPS the RCD (=> element earth leakage)

commonConfusion.name: too hot = the element is too powerful
commonConfusion.note: The element receives power according to the control system - an oven running too hot is the THERMOSTAT/sensor/control not regulating, not an over-powerful element.
wouldApplyIf: temperature far above the setting, never cycling off

commonConfusion.name: cuts out when hot = thermostat
commonConfusion.note: Cuts out hot and recovers when cool can be the COOLING FAN / airflow / thermal cutout. Cuts out WITH an RCD trip is element earth leakage. Only a non-tripping thermal regulation fault is the thermostat.
wouldApplyIf: cuts out hot without tripping and without the cooling fan/airflow being implicated

discriminators: Burns everything / runs too hot even on low / never cycles off => the temperature is NOT being regulated: mechanical dial-thermostat oven => oven thermostat (and its capillary/phial); electronic oven => temperature sensor + control. It is NOT an over-powerful element.

Cuts out / goes cold once hot WITHOUT tripping the electrics => thermostat or overheat thermal cutout - and consider the COOLING FAN (if it recovers when cool). If it TRIPS THE RCD, that's an element earth fault (tripping-electrics), not the thermostat.
ARCHITECTURE: don't recommend a mechanical thermostat on a sensor/electronic oven or vice-versa - identify the control type.
adviceBeforeReplacement: check whether the temperature is far above the setting and whether it ever cycles off
establish whether it TRIPS the electrics (element) or just goes cold (thermostat/cutout/cooling fan)
oven-cooker:thermostat.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:thermostat.clarifyingQuestion: Is it running much too hot (burning even on low), or does it go cold after a while - and does it trip the electrics when it does?
oven-cooker:thermostat.secondaryQuestion: Is it a dial-thermostat oven or an electronic one with a digital temperature display?

oven-cooker:clock-timer._approved: Flashing programmer after power loss is a control-state/use-condition (ADVICE_ONLY). Do not surface parts until MANUAL operation is restored or ruled out.
symptoms: oven wont come on but the clock works
oven wont turn on since a power cut
wont start until the clock is set

components.name: clock/timer set to AUTO - set to MANUAL (free fix)
supports: stopped after a power cut / power switched off
clock flashing or showing AUTO/A
oven won't run but the display works, hob/grill may still work
against: clock correctly set to MANUAL and the oven still won't heat (=> element/supply)

components.name: timer / programmer module (genuine failure)
supports: can't set the clock at all / buttons or segments faulty
output never enables the oven despite correct MANUAL setting
display itself faulty
against: simply reset to AUTO after a power cut (set it to manual - no part)

commonConfusion.name: dead after power cut = replace the timer
commonConfusion.note: Almost never a faulty part. The clock reset and the oven won't run in AUTO. Set it to MANUAL (hand symbol) and the time. Don't switch it off at the wall (that resets AUTO again).
wouldApplyIf: it works once set to MANUAL - then there is no fault

discriminators: THIS IS A CONTROL-STATE / USE-CONDITION, NOT A PART. After a power interruption the clock/programmer often defaults into automatic/timed operation and the oven will not heat until returned to MANUAL. Lead with that advice. Do not recommend a timer, PCB or element, and do not ask for the model to sell a part, until MANUAL has been restored or ruled out.
Only if the oven STILL will not heat once in MANUAL, or the clock genuinely cannot be set, is a timer/programmer even a component hypothesis — still not automatically a purchase.
adviceBeforeReplacement: set the clock/timer to MANUAL (hand symbol) and the correct time first
do not switch off at the wall to 'reset' it - that just puts it back to AUTO
oven-cooker:clock-timer.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:clock-timer.clarifyingQuestion: On the clock, is there an AUTO/A showing - can you switch it to the MANUAL (hand) symbol and set the time?

oven-cooker:main-pcb._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). Control/programmer/display + generic dead - but PCB is LAST. Dead => check supply/terminal-block and the clock-AUTO free-fix first. Display/comms issues route here.

components.name: external supply / isolator (completely dead)
supports: completely dead - check the cooker switch/isolator and house circuit first
against: supply proven live

components.name: clock/timer set to AUTO (power-cut free fix)
supports: won't come on but the clock/display works, especially after a power cut - timer reset to AUTO
against: display itself dead/blank

components.name: mains terminal block / incoming connection
supports: dead with a burning smell / heat damage at the mains connection (=> terminal-block)
against: no heat damage; a clean electronic display fault

components.name: display / user interface
supports: display blank/garbled but the oven otherwise has power
against: completely dead including no light (=> supply/terminal-block)

components.name: main control PCB / programmer
supports: supply, terminal-block, clock-setting and display proven good and it still won't respond
customers may call this the programmer/brain/module
against: cheaper causes (supply/terminal/clock/display) not excluded

commonConfusion.name: dead oven = PCB
commonConfusion.note: Down-rank the PCB. Completely dead => check the supply/isolator, the mains terminal block (burning?), and the clock-AUTO free-fix first.
wouldApplyIf: supply, terminal-block and clock-setting all proven good

commonConfusion.name: won't come on after a power cut = failed board
commonConfusion.note: Usually the clock/timer reset to AUTO - set it to MANUAL (hand symbol) first.
wouldApplyIf: clock/display works but the oven won't run; fixed once set to manual? then no fault

discriminators: Customers call the control board the 'programmer', 'brain' or 'module' - all mean the main PCB. It is the LAST candidate.

OVEN DEAD is ambiguous: establish display/clock, flashing/AUTO, fan/light, any heating function, and recent power interruption before a board or element. COMPLETELY DEAD (no display, no light) => supply/isolator, then mains TERMINAL BLOCK, then wiring; PCB last. DISPLAY works but oven won't run, especially after a power cut => programmer AUTO — MANUAL first, not a board.
DISPLAY blank/garbled with power present => display/UI; only then the PCB.
adviceBeforeReplacement: completely dead: check the cooker switch/isolator and house circuit; check for a burning smell at the mains connection
after a power cut set the clock/timer to MANUAL before condemning the board

Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:main-pcb.clarifyingQuestion: Is it completely dead (no display, no light), or does the display work but the oven won't heat?

microwave:door._poc: Story 4 POC — richer diagnostic knowledge for the MECHANICAL 'door physically won't open' symptom. Represents per-candidate evidence FOR/AGAINST and treats the interlock microswitch as common-confusion (electrical, not mechanical). Approved engineer assessment; do not extrapolate to other nodes.
symptoms: button does nothing when i press it
acts like the door is open
wont start with the door closed

components.name: door release button / lever / linkage
supports: the button moves but doesn't release the door
the button feels loose or floppy
the button resistance has suddenly changed
the button has excessive travel
pressing at a particular angle sometimes releases the door
the release action disappeared suddenly
against: the release button feels mechanically normal
the button/lever clearly operates the latch mechanism
the symptom is electrical rather than physical (door closes fine but won't start)

components.name: door latch / hook mechanism
supports: the release button feels reasonably normal but the door stays caught
the door had become progressively harder to open
the door needs movement/lifting/pressure before it releases
the latch/hook appears damaged, worn or misaligned
an abnormal mechanical click or feel around the latch
against: the release button/linkage is obviously loose, broken or not transmitting movement
the door physically opens and closes normally and the real complaint is that it won't operate

components.name: button / latch return spring
supports: the button doesn't return normally
the button stays depressed
the mechanism feels unusually slack
the release behaviour changed suddenly
against: the button returns with normal resistance and movement
the evidence points to the latch/hook binding further along the mechanism

components.name: door alignment / hinge / accessible obstruction
supports: the door needs lifting or moving to release
the door appears dropped or misaligned
the problem became progressively worse
visible debris or grease around the accessible latch area
the door became increasingly difficult to open before eventually sticking
against: sudden failure together with a loose/floppy release button
an obviously broken release linkage

components.name: door interlock / monitor microswitch (electrical start path)
supports: the door CLOSES normally but the microwave WON'T START (beeps / acts as though the door is open)
intermittent start when the door is nudged
the latch engages but the switch isn't being made
against: the door physically WON'T OPEN/RELEASE (mechanical)
the release button feels loose/floppy or the handle is broken (mechanical)

discriminators: SYMPTOM SPLIT: a door that physically WON'T OPEN/RELEASE is a MECHANICAL fault - lead with the release button/lever/linkage, then the latch/hook, the return spring, and alignment/hinge/obstruction. A door that CLOSES normally but the microwave WON'T START (beeps, acts like the door is open) is the ELECTRICAL interlock path - only then is the interlock/monitor microswitch a leading suspect. Do NOT lead with the interlock microswitch for a purely mechanical won't-open complaint.

BUTTON FEEL is the strongest discriminator: LOOSE/FLOPPY button = broken release button/lever/linkage or its spring/connection; NORMAL button but door still caught = latch/hook or alignment/binding further along; UNUSUALLY STIFF/JAMMED = binding latch/lever, an obstruction, or alignment. Use as evidence to re-rank, not as a guarantee.

TEMPORARY post-cooking sticking (hard to open just after cooking, releases normally shortly after) is a low-frequency pattern - do NOT treat it as a broken mechanical release; clarify before recommending a part.
adviceBeforeReplacement: the customer can visually inspect the accessible latch area
accessible crumbs/debris/grease around the latch can be gently cleaned
do not force or pry the door open
do not remove the microwave casing
do not test internal interlock switches and never bypass an interlock
microwave:door.clarifyingQuestion: When you press the door-release button, does it feel normal, loose/floppy, or unusually stiff?
microwave:door.secondaryQuestion: Did it become harder to open over time, or did it suddenly stop opening?

microwave:turntable._approved: Story 21 — engineer-approved (microwave completion). CHECK tray seating/obstruction/roller first; distinguish motor-not-driving from coupler-not-transmitting. A smashed glass tray is a direct accessory, not a motor diagnosis. Don't jump to the PCB.

components.name: tray seated correctly / obstruction
supports: tray not sitting on the coupler/rollers properly
something jamming the plate
food/debris under the tray
against: tray correctly seated and clear, still won't turn

components.name: roller ring / support wheels
supports: worn/dirty roller wheels
the ring dislodged or clogged
against: roller ring clean and intact

components.name: turntable coupler
supports: the motor turns/hums but the plate doesn't (drive not transmitted)
a stripped/split coupler
against: nothing moves at all and the motor is silent

components.name: turntable motor
supports: no movement at all and the motor is silent/dead with the tray removed
the coupler is intact but nothing drives it
against: the motor clearly turns but the plate doesn't (=> coupler)

components.name: glass turntable plate (if smashed)
supports: the glass plate/tray is smashed or cracked - a direct replacement accessory
against: the plate is intact but won't turn (=> coupler/motor/roller)

commonConfusion.name: turntable fault = main PCB
commonConfusion.note: Don't jump to the PCB. Check seating/obstruction/roller, then the coupler, then the motor.
wouldApplyIf: seating, roller, coupler and motor all proven good

commonConfusion.name: smashed glass = motor diagnosis
commonConfusion.note: A broken glass tray is a direct accessory purchase (glass turntable), not a motor fault - don't send it through the motor path.
wouldApplyIf: the customer says the glass plate is smashed/broken

discriminators: CHECK the tray is seated on the coupler/rollers, clear of obstruction, and the roller ring is intact/clean FIRST. Then distinguish MOTOR NOT DRIVING (nothing moves, motor silent) from COUPLER NOT TRANSMITTING (motor turns/hums but the plate doesn't). Don't jump to the PCB.
A SMASHED/CRACKED glass plate is a direct accessory (glass turntable), NOT a fault-diagnosis - identify the replacement tray, don't run a motor diagnosis.
adviceBeforeReplacement: reseat the tray on the coupler/rollers and clear any obstruction
check the roller ring/wheels are clean and intact
if the glass plate is smashed, that's just a replacement tray
microwave:turntable.safety: ADVISORY ONLY: unplug before inspecting; HV stored charge - stay in the accessible cavity.
microwave:turntable.clarifyingQuestion: When it should turn, does the motor hum/try to turn while the plate stays still, or is there no movement or sound at all - or is the glass plate actually broken?
microwave:turntable.secondaryQuestion: Is the tray seated properly on the coupler and rollers, with nothing jamming it?

symptoms: trips as soon as i turn it on
discriminators: 'Knocking the electrics out', 'flipping the fuse box', 'tripping the mains' all mean it trips the RCD/fuse - an earth fault.

Trips once it starts HEATING (fills then trips a few minutes in) = the HEATER ELEMENT leaking to earth (most common). Trips the instant it's switched on or as it fills = a wiring/short or a shorted DRAIN PUMP or mains lead. Water getting into wiring/connectors can also trip it.
Isolate by timing: which part of the cycle trips it (fill, heat, wash, spin)? That points to heater vs motor vs pump.
adviceBeforeReplacement: do NOT keep resetting the RCD/breaker and re-running an appliance that repeatedly trips the supply - stop use where there is a credible electrical fault
note the timing of the trip (on power / on fill / when heating starts / on spin) to localise the fault before replacing a part
washing-machine:tripping-electrics.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): an appliance that repeatedly trips the electrics should be taken out of use - do not repeatedly reset the breaker to keep testing it.
washing-machine:tripping-electrics.clarifyingQuestion: At what point does it trip - as soon as you switch it on, once it starts heating, or on spin?

safetyInformation.text: An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
safetyInformation.hazard: Dangerous wiring or an insulation fault (repeated tripping, a burning smell or scorch marks); water present raises shock risk.
safetyInformation.applicability: Appliance repeatedly trips the electrics, or there is a burning smell / scorching.

washing-machine:dispenser._approved: Story 16 — engineer-reviewed DISPENSER / soap-drawer assessment. The dispenser is part of a WATER-DELIVERY system: adequate incoming water -> reaching the dispenser -> correct compartment flow -> can it leave -> only then a failed part. Conditioner uses a SIPHON. Auto-dose is architecture-conditional. CHECK before PART.
symptoms: water only trickles into the drawer
water down the front from the drawer

components.name: property water pressure / cold supply
supports: ALL compartments flush weakly / water only trickles in
fill is generally slow
poor supply or recent supply change
against: only ONE compartment affected (others flush fine)
water clearly enters the compartment but product remains

components.name: isolation tap / inlet hose restriction
supports: tap only part-open or hose kinked/crushed (all-compartment weak flow)
machine recently moved
against: good flow demonstrated and only one compartment affected

components.name: inlet-valve inlet filter / strainer
supports: property pressure good and hose clear but flow into the drawer is weak (all compartments)
silted inlet strainer
against: filter clear and poor flow remains (valve)
single-compartment problem

components.name: detergent use — type / amount / compartment / liquid insert / congealed
supports: good water enters but powder/detergent remains
liquid detergent used in the drawer, sticky/caked
wrong compartment or missing liquid-detergent insert/flap
too much detergent
against: no/low water is actually reaching the compartment (delivery path)

components.name: conditioner siphon cap / insert / channel / jets
supports: WATER ENTERS the conditioner compartment but conditioner/water REMAINS afterwards
siphon cap/insert missing or misfitted
blocked jets/channel or residue/congealed softener
softener above the MAX line or too thick
against: NO water reaches the conditioner compartment (water-delivery path to it)

components.name: drawer / dispenser roof jets & channels (clean; replace only if damaged)
supports: visible residue/limescale/mould blocking drawer passages or roof jets
product remains despite adequate water
against: drawer clean and clear but flow still poor (upstream) or won't discharge (dispenser-to-tub)

components.name: auto-dose settings / reservoir / concentration / cleaning [auto-dose machines ONLY]
supports: auto-dosing machine
auto-dose turned off / dose-per-wash not set (often OFF by default or after a power cut)
reservoir empty / wrong or congealed product
concentration setting doesn't match the product
needs a dispenser clean / self-clean
against: conventional drawer machine with no auto-dose system

components.name: inlet valve (partially opening / restricted / one coil-path)
supports: property pressure good AND hose/inlet filter clear but flow still weak (a valve can partly open and pass only a trickle)
long fill time
on a multi-coil valve one compartment path is weak while another is fine
against: upstream restriction (tap/hose/filter) not excluded
water clearly reaches the compartment but product remains (siphon/jets/use)

components.name: dispenser-to-tub hose / discharge path
supports: water REACHES the drawer but can't discharge - drawer overflows / backs up / leaks down the front during fill
split/displaced/blocked discharge path
against: problem is getting water INTO the drawer (upstream supply/valve/channel)

components.name: water distributor / diverter [architectures that use one]
supports: one compartment gets NO water while others work AND the design uses a mechanical/electronic distributor/diverter
distributor not directing water to that compartment
against: no such distributor on this design (single/multi-coil valve feeds fixed channels)
local jet/channel blockage explains it

components.name: auto-dose pump [auto-dose machines ONLY]
supports: confirmed auto-dose machine, settings/reservoir/cleaning all good, but product still not dosed
against: conventional machine with no auto-dose pump - do NOT recommend
settings/reservoir/concentration/cleaning not yet checked

components.name: dispenser assembly (damaged)
supports: drawer/dispenser physically cracked/damaged and cleaning won't restore it
against: a clean/use/blockage cause not yet excluded

components.name: wiring / control PCB
supports: supply good, passages clear, architecture known, and the expected valve/diverter is not being commanded/operated
against: any physical/hydraulic/use cause remains

commonConfusion.name: soap-drawer problem = replace the dispenser
commonConfusion.note: The dispenser is part of a water-delivery system. Exclude incoming water/pressure, the delivery path, blockages, siphon and detergent use before recommending a dispenser/valve/PCB part.
wouldApplyIf: the drawer/dispenser is physically damaged and cleaning won't restore it

commonConfusion.name: conditioner remains = inlet valve / no water
commonConfusion.note: If water clearly ENTERED the conditioner compartment but it remains, the incoming supply is LESS suspicious - raise the siphon cap/insert, blocked jets/channel, residue, or softener above MAX / too thick. Conditioner is drawn by a siphon on the final rinse.
wouldApplyIf: NO water reaches the conditioner compartment at all (then investigate the delivery path to it)

commonConfusion.name: all compartments weak = dispenser fault
commonConfusion.note: General weak flow across the whole drawer points to incoming water (property pressure -> tap/hose -> inlet filter -> a partially-opening inlet valve), not a local dispenser fault (cross-ref Story-10 filling).
wouldApplyIf: only one compartment is affected while others flush normally

commonConfusion.name: loads of foam from the drawer = failed dispenser
commonConfusion.note: Excess foam out of the drawer is usually a detergent-use/oversudsing issue - cross-ref foam-suds, not a broken dispenser.
wouldApplyIf: a genuine dispensing/flow fault persists with correct detergent and no excess foam

commonConfusion.name: water not going where expected = PCB
commonConfusion.note: Physical/hydraulic/use causes come first. Only raise control/PCB once supply is good, passages are clear, the architecture is known and the expected valve/diverter isn't being operated.
wouldApplyIf: all physical causes excluded and the expected actuator isn't commanded

commonConfusion.name: auto-dose pump on a conventional machine
commonConfusion.note: Only propose an auto-dose pump/reservoir on machines whose architecture actually has automatic dosing. Establish conventional-drawer vs auto-dose first.
wouldApplyIf: the model is confirmed to have an automatic-dosing system

discriminators: WATER-DELIVERY CHAIN: is there adequate incoming water? -> is it reaching the dispenser? -> is the correct compartment getting adequate flow? -> can that water/product leave? Only THEN a failed valve/distributor/dispenser part.
KEY: when it should take detergent/conditioner, does PLENTY of water enter that compartment, just a TRICKLE, or NONE? (adequate-but-not-emptying vs low-flow vs no-flow).
ALL compartments weak / trickle => property pressure -> isolation tap/hose -> inlet filter -> partially-opening inlet valve (Story-10), BEFORE local dispenser faults.
ONE compartment fails, others work => local jet/channel/siphon or an architecture-specific distributor/diverter/valve path; generic property pressure moves DOWN.

CONDITIONER remains BUT water entered => siphon cap/insert/channel/jets, residue, softener above MAX / too thick - NOT the inlet valve (water demonstrably reached it). Conditioner is siphon-drawn on the final rinse.
CONDITIONER gets NO water (others fine) => the water-delivery path to that compartment (jet/channel/diverter).
POWDER remains: little/no water => delivery path; good water but powder remains => caking / too much / wrong or liquid detergent / blocked drawer.

OVERFLOW / down the front => direction matters: no water IN = upstream supply/valve/channel; water IN but can't LEAVE = drawer/siphon/dispenser-to-tub path. Cross-ref leak-flood; loads of foam => foam-suds.
LIQUID detergent in the drawer can cake/congeal - establish powder vs liquid, correct compartment, and any liquid insert/flap; clean, don't replace.

AUTO-DOSE (architecture): first establish conventional-drawer vs auto-dose. Auto-dose CHECKS: enabled / dose set (often OFF by default or after a power cut), reservoir has the right product, concentration set to match, congealed detergent, air-pocket, needs cleaning/self-clean - pump/control only if the architecture confirms one and checks fail.
PCB / dispenser assembly are NOT default fallbacks - exclude physical/hydraulic/use causes first.
adviceBeforeReplacement: clean the drawer, the conditioner siphon cap/insert and the roof jets (soak removable parts in warm water; scrub the jet holes and channels)
check the conditioner/detergent isn't above the MAX line or too thick (dilute thick softener; don't exceed MAX)
check the correct compartment is used and any liquid-detergent insert/flap is fitted
if ALL compartments are weak, check the taps, inlet hose and inlet filter/strainer before the valve (cross-ref filling)
on an auto-dosing machine, check it's switched on and dosed, the reservoir has the right product and the concentration matches, and run a dispenser/self-clean
switch off/unplug and isolate the water before removing the inlet hose or filter to inspect
washing-machine:dispenser.safety: ADVISORY ONLY: switch off/unplug and isolate the water before removing hoses/filters for inspection. No live-voltage testing, energised-valve testing or interlock bypass - this is diagnostic knowledge, not a repair manual.
washing-machine:dispenser.clarifyingQuestion: When it should take the detergent or conditioner, does plenty of water enter that compartment, just a trickle, or no water at all?
washing-machine:dispenser.secondaryQuestion: Is it only one compartment (like the conditioner section) or are all of them flushing poorly - and is it a conventional drawer or an automatic-dosing machine?

washing-machine:not-draining._approved: Story 9 — engineer-reviewed drainage assessment. Distinguishes diagnostic CHECKS (clean/clear first, not a part sale) from replacement PARTS.
symptoms: wont spin with water in the drum
makes a noise but no water comes out
it drains but water comes back up
sink backs up when it drains

components.name: blocked pump filter / foreign object in the pump path
supports: water remains in the drum
draining became progressively slower
a drain error is shown
the pump can be heard trying to drain
rattling/noisy pump during drain
debris/foreign object found in the accessible filter/pump area
against: filter and accessible pump path confirmed clear
drain hose/outlet confirmed clear
evidence the pump isn't being driven electrically

components.name: blocked / kinked drain hose or waste connection
supports: pump can be heard running but little/no water leaves
drainage is slow
machine recently moved or reinstalled
drain hose kinked/crushed
waste connection/standpipe obstructed
against: the complete drain path has been shown free-flowing
the pump isn't running
the obstruction appears to be before the pump

components.name: drain pump obstructed / jammed or failed
supports: filter clear AND external drain path clear
pump hums but moves no water
pump unusually noisy
intermittent draining
impeller obstructed/jammed
pump silent when drain is commanded, after simpler causes are excluded
against: pump is moving water normally
a restriction exists elsewhere (filter/hose/waste)

components.name: internal sump hose / obstruction before the pump
supports: accessible filter clear AND external path clear
poor/no water flow into the pump
suspected garment/foreign-object obstruction
intermittent or partial drainage
against: water reaches the pump freely
an external restriction has been identified
clear evidence of electrical pump failure

components.name: pressure system / water-level sensing
supports: abnormal water-level behaviour
unusual drain sequencing
repeated/inappropriate draining
mechanical drain path and pump don't explain the symptoms
against: obvious filter/hose blockage
jammed pump
a confirmed failed drain pump

components.name: control PCB / wiring to the pump
supports: pump and drainage path shown good
pump not energised when drain is commanded
relevant wiring/connector evidence
associated control abnormalities
against: simpler hydraulic/mechanical causes not yet excluded

commonConfusion.name: drain pump (as an automatic replacement)
commonConfusion.note: 'Not draining' does NOT mean a failed drain pump. Pump running/humming with no drainage does not automatically mean replace the pump - a blockage/restriction (filter, hose, sump, foreign object) must stay high in the diagnosis and be excluded first.
wouldApplyIf: filter clear AND external drain path clear AND (pump hums but no water, or pump silent) after simpler causes are excluded

commonConfusion.name: motor / belt / spin components
commonConfusion.note: Spin is inhibited until the machine has emptied, so 'won't spin' WITH water still in the drum is usually a DRAINAGE problem, not a motor/belt fault. Only treat as a spin/motor fault when NO water remains.
wouldApplyIf: customer says won't spin AND the drum is empty (no retained water)

discriminators: WON'T SPIN + WATER STILL IN THE DRUM = investigate DRAINAGE first (spin is inhibited until emptied); do NOT jump to motor/belt/spin parts. WON'T SPIN + NO retained water = not a drainage fault, see motor-drum.

FREE FIX FIRST: the most common cause is a BLOCKED PUMP FILTER or a trapped foreign object (coins, hair grips, buttons, lint) - clear/clean the filter and accessible pump path before condemning the drain pump. This is a CHECK, not a part.
PUMP HUMMING + NO DRAINAGE does NOT automatically mean replace the pump: a blocked filter/hose/sump or a jammed impeller gives the same sound. Exclude blockages first.

If filter, hose, waste and any trapped object are all clear and the pump hums-but-moves-nothing or is silent when commanded, THEN it's the drain pump (jammed/failed) or, with abnormal level behaviour, the pressure system.
Slow/progressive drainage or a recent house move points to a hose/waste restriction rather than a failed pump.

DRAINS OK BUT DIRTY WATER BACKS UP / RETURNS (into the drum, or up through the sink or standpipe), especially with a DRAIN or SEWER SMELL: the machine IS pumping out - the fault is in the HOUSEHOLD WASTE PLUMBING (a blocked standpipe, waste trap/U-bend, or the kitchen sink waste the drain hose empties into), NOT the appliance pump, filter or hose. Advise checking/clearing the standpipe and household waste plumbing; do not condemn or sell a drain pump for this. A machine that simply WON'T EMPTY at all is still the appliance - see the filter/pump above.
adviceBeforeReplacement: if the machine still holds water, follow the appliance's safe residual-water draining procedure/manual FIRST - opening the pump filter with water inside can release a large amount of water
inspect and clean the accessible pump filter where the model design allows
check the drain hose for kinks/crushing and the waste connection/standpipe for blockage (especially if the machine was recently moved)
clear any trapped foreign object in the accessible pump path before recommending a replacement pump
washing-machine:not-draining.clarifyingQuestion: Is there still water sitting in the drum, and when it tries to drain can you hear the pump running or humming?
washing-machine:not-draining.secondaryQuestion: Did the draining get gradually slower over time or stop suddenly, and has the machine been moved or reinstalled recently?

Establish truly-dead vs powered-won't-start first; external supply before appliance parts; incoming-power path (mains filter -> wiring -> power switch) BEFORE the PCB. Blown fuse is EVIDENCE, not the fix. No electrical-test instructions. CHECK vs PART preserved.

commonConfusion.name: powered-but-won't-start = dead
commonConfusion.note: If the display/lights work and a programme can be selected but pressing Start does nothing, the machine is NOT dead - the door interlock / start-permission / control-lock path is the leading route (see door-lock). Don't let 'won't start' become 'dead/no power'.
wouldApplyIf: there are genuinely NO lights/display/response at all

commonConfusion.name: display dead but the machine still responds/runs = total power loss
commonConfusion.note: A failed display/UI module or its connection can leave the display blank while the rest of the machine still works - that is a UI/display fault (see control-panel/comms), not a loss of appliance power.
wouldApplyIf: there is truly no power anywhere (no response at all)

commonConfusion.name: dead = replace the control PCB
commonConfusion.note: Do not lead with the PCB because the machine is dead. Exclude the external supply, plug/lead, mains filter and incoming wiring first; the PCB power-supply section is an evidence-based last conclusion.
wouldApplyIf: supply, lead, mains filter and wiring are all confirmed good and it's still dead

commonConfusion.name: blown plug fuse = replace the fuse and it's fixed
commonConfusion.note: A blown fuse is EVIDENCE, not automatically the fault - ask WHY it blew. Replacing it may restore power without addressing the cause. A healthy fuse doesn't prove there's no fault (RCD/MCB may operate first). Do NOT repeatedly replace fuses or carry out electrical testing.
wouldApplyIf: the fuse blew with no underlying electrical fault (e.g. a genuinely one-off event) - which cannot be assumed

discriminators: ESTABLISH TRULY DEAD FIRST: absolutely no lights/display/response = dead/no-power family; powers up and lets you select a programme but won't Start = door-lock/start-permission (see door-lock), NOT dead.

EXTERNAL SUPPLY FIRST for a truly dead machine: does the socket work with another device, is any switched/fused spur on, is the plug/lead seated? Recent house move / machine move raises supply/installation strongly. These are CHECKS, not appliance parts.

CONFIRMED SUPPLY + STILL DEAD: work the incoming-power path - mains interference suppressor/filter (first component powered) -> incoming wiring/connector -> power switch (if fitted) -> PCB low-voltage power-supply LAST. Do not rank the PCB first.

BLOWN FUSE = ask WHY it blew (evidence, not the fix). Do not instruct repeated fuse replacement, live testing, insulation/earth-leakage testing or bypassing protection - that's beyond WhichPart; advise professional electrical diagnosis if needed.

TIMING (use already-observed behaviour, don't ask them to reproduce an electrical fault): dead from the outset => incoming supply/filter/wiring/PCB; died around the HEATING stage => the heater circuit deserves strong consideration (high-current, in contact with water) but not certainty - cross-ref heater/tripping-electrics; died when the MOTOR/drum started => motor/drive electrical path (motor-drum); died at another repeatable stage => the component active at that stage.

INTERMITTENTLY DEAD (comes back later, responds to disturbing the plug/lead) => loose/burnt connection, mains lead, filter, power switch or a thermal/intermittent PCB power fault - distinct from permanently dead. Do NOT tell the customer to manipulate wiring/connections while powered.

BURNING SMELL / POP / BANG then dead => mains filter, burnt connector/wiring, PCB/power electronics, or another component causing secondary electrical damage - do NOT equate a burning smell with the PCB. Stop-use safety applies.
adviceBeforeReplacement: check the socket works with another appliance and that any separate switched/fused spur controlling it is on (especially after a recent move)
check the plug is fully seated and the lead undamaged - vibration can work a plug loose over time
if there was a pop/bang/burning smell, or any sign of burnt wiring, stop using it and unplug it
a blown plug fuse is a clue - the underlying cause needs finding; do not just keep replacing fuses, and leave electrical testing to a professional
washing-machine:low-voltage.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): a burning smell, pop/bang, smoke or burnt wiring means stop use and unplug. WhichPart identifies WHAT is likely wrong and WHY - it does not provide live-testing, insulation/earth-leakage testing, protection-bypass or repeated-fuse-replacement instructions; recommend a professional for electrical diagnosis where needed.
washing-machine:low-voltage.clarifyingQuestion: Is it completely dead with no lights or display at all, or does it power up and let you choose a programme but then not start?
washing-machine:low-voltage.secondaryQuestion: Do other nearby sockets have power, and has the machine or your home recently been moved or had a power cut?

mediaInformation.title: About the door lock (interlock)
mediaInformation.description: The door lock (interlock) keeps the door shut during a wash and stops the machine starting unless the door is locked. This reference shows where it sits. empty, cool, past the delay, handle normal, but the lock genuinely won't release

against: retained water or a normal unlock delay explains it
the handle/catch is physically broken (mechanical)
truly dead with no lights/display (see low-voltage)

components.name: wiring / connector to the lock
supports: intermittent door error with an otherwise-good lock
loose/burnt connector to the lock

components.name: control PCB
supports: door physically fine, interlock and wiring proven good, water/level normal, but the lock isn't commanded

commonConfusion.name: door won't open = failed interlock
commonConfusion.note: First ask WHY the machine is keeping it locked: retained water, an unfinished programme, still hot, or the normal unlock delay - and whether the handle/catch is physically broken. A correctly-working lock stays engaged until conditions are safe.
wouldApplyIf: empty, cool, past the delay, handle works normally, and the lock genuinely won't release

commonConfusion.name: broken handle = failed electrical interlock
commonConfusion.note: A physically broken/floppy handle or catch can stop the door releasing even when the electrical lock is working perfectly. Broken handle => mechanical part, not the interlock.
wouldApplyIf: there is independent evidence the interlock also failed

commonConfusion.name: locked door + water in drum = door fault
commonConfusion.note: The lock is probably doing its job - protecting you from opening onto water. Diagnose the DRAINAGE / water-level cause first (see not-draining); do not force the door or replace the lock.
wouldApplyIf: the drum is empty yet the door stays locked

commonConfusion.name: won't start = dead / no power
commonConfusion.note: If the display/lights work and a programme can be selected but Start does nothing, the machine has power - route to door interlock / start-permission (Story 15), not dead/low-voltage.
wouldApplyIf: there are genuinely no lights/display/response (see low-voltage)

commonConfusion.name: control PCB as the fallback for a door problem
commonConfusion.note: Don't lead with the PCB just because the lock is electronically controlled. Physical engagement, the interlock and its wiring come first.
wouldApplyIf: door physically fine, interlock and wiring proven good, but the lock isn't commanded

commonConfusion.name: door seal because the complaint mentions 'door'
commonConfusion.note: A door seal is not normally why a machine electrically refuses to start. Trapped clothing or a badly displaced seal can physically prevent closure, but don't let the word 'door' over-rank the seal (see leak-flood for seal leaks).
wouldApplyIf: clothing/displaced seal is physically stopping the door closing

discriminators: There are TWO separate systems: a mechanical spring-loaded latch/catch that holds the door physically shut, and a SEPARATE electrical interlock that locks it during operation. Match the candidate to which one the evidence points at.
WATER IN DRUM + LOCKED => drainage / water-level FIRST (Story 9); the lock is likely protecting the customer. Do not force it or replace the lock.
JUST FINISHED / STILL HOT => a normal timed safety/unlock delay can hold it for a minute or two - wait before diagnosing a part. (Don't encode one maker's exact timing.)
EMPTY + COOL + HANDLE FLOPPY/BROKEN => MECHANICAL release/handle/catch/linkage leads; the electrical interlock is down-ranked.
PHYSICALLY WON'T CLOSE => obstruction/trapped clothing/overload/alignment/catch/hinge first, not the electrical lock.
CLOSES NORMALLY + POWERED + PROGRAMMABLE + WON'T START => electrical interlock / start-permission (NOT dead/no-power, Story 15).
STARTS ONLY IF THE DOOR IS PUSHED/LIFTED => hinge/alignment / worn catch / poor interlock engagement - argues AGAINST a generic PCB or power fault.
EMPTY but the controller behaves as though WATER REMAINS => a pressure/water-level false signal can hold the lock (see pressure-switch) - consider before replacing the lock.
Only once retained water, unlock delay, mechanical handle/catch and control-lock are excluded is a failed interlock/lock the answer.

ALREADY REPLACED the door lock / interlock and it STILL won't start? The new lock is proven, so move to the WIRING / loom to the interlock and the MAIN PCB (the control isn't sending or confirming the lock signal). Do NOT re-blame the lock, and do NOT default to the 'cycle didn't complete' explanation - that is for a door that won't OPEN after a wash, not a won't-START.
adviceBeforeReplacement: if the door won't open, first check whether there's still water in the drum and whether the cycle actually finished - do not force a door with water in it
if it's just finished or still hot, wait a couple of minutes for the safety lock to release before suspecting a part
check a control-lock/child-lock isn't on and the programme isn't paused
if it won't close, check for trapped washing around the seal, an overloaded drum, or an obstruction around the catch
if the drum is empty and cool, check whether the handle feels normal or loose/floppy before deciding mechanical vs electrical
use the machine's model-specific emergency-release procedure if provided; do not force the door, defeat the interlock, or open it onto water
washing-machine:door-lock.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): never force a locked door, especially with water in the drum or while the machine/water may be hot; unplug/isolate before mechanical access; do not bypass or defeat the door interlock, and emergency-release procedures vary by model (no generic bypass). No live electrical testing.
washing-machine:door-lock.clarifyingQuestion: Is the door physically stuck shut, or does it close normally but the machine won't start - and is there still water in the drum?
washing-machine:door-lock.secondaryQuestion: If it's stuck shut: is the drum empty and does the handle feel normal or loose/floppy? If it won't start: does the door seem to lock when you press Start?

commonConfusion.name: heating element (as the automatic answer to 'not heating')
commonConfusion.note: 'Not heating = element' is too simplistic. The element produces heat, but sensing (NTC), switching (relay/control), wiring and the machine's sequence all determine whether it actually heats. Confirm a genuine no-heat first.
wouldApplyIf: genuine hot programme, fills/tumbles normally, reaches heating stage, target temperature not reached, and the NTC/wiring are not the stronger explanation

commonConfusion.name: cold laundry / cool door = heater failed
commonConfusion.note: Weak evidence on its own: final rinses are cold, eco/low-temp programmes heat little, and finished laundry naturally feels cool. Clarify the programme/temperature and how they judged it before recommending a part.
wouldApplyIf: there is objective evidence beyond cool laundry/door (stalls in wash, error, cold on a genuine hot wash)

commonConfusion.name: machine stuck on wash = control PCB
commonConfusion.note: On programme logic that waits for the target wash temperature, a heating failure often makes the machine REMAIN in wash (waiting for a temperature it never reaches). Fills+tumbles normally but washes for hours => raise the heating system, do not default to the PCB. (Common, not universal across platforms.)
wouldApplyIf: fill normal, tumble normal, drainage not blocking, stuck specifically in wash/heating at a consistent point

commonConfusion.name: the NTC heats the water
commonConfusion.note: It does not. The NTC is a negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor whose resistance changes with temperature; it provides temperature FEEDBACK to the controller. A faulty NTC can cause no/incorrect heat, overheating, or failure to progress - via wrong feedback, not by heating.
wouldApplyIf: heater appears serviceable but temperature feedback/behaviour is implausible or intermittent

commonConfusion.name: broken heater = just replace the heater
commonConfusion.note: On front-entry-heater designs a broken heater SUPPORT/BRACKET lets the heater move and contact the drum/tub, damaging it. If mechanically damaged, inspect the support and find WHY - otherwise a replacement heater may be damaged again.
wouldApplyIf: front-entry-heater design with mechanical damage to the heater

commonConfusion.name: sometimes completes so the heater must work (hot/cold-fill machines)
commonConfusion.note: On OLDER machines with SEPARATE hot and cold inlets, incoming hot water can occasionally be warm enough to reach the progression threshold despite a failed internal heater; on cooler cycles it sticks. Intermittent progression does NOT exclude a failed heater on hot/cold-fill machines. Do not apply to modern cold-fill-only machines.
wouldApplyIf: architecture confirmed as separate hot-and-cold fill, with variable progression and a suspected heater

discriminators: SUSPECTED vs CONFIRMED: cold laundry or a cool door/glass alone is WEAK evidence (cold rinses, eco/low-temp, judged at the wrong point) - clarify programme/temperature first, do not recommend a heater. Genuine no-heat needs evidence it should be heating and isn't.

STUCK ON WASH: fills normally + tumbles normally + stays in wash abnormally long / won't progress => strongly raise the HEATING SYSTEM (the controller is typically waiting for a target temperature it isn't reaching). Common programme behaviour, not universal - and rule out slow fill / drainage delay / load first.

ELEMENT vs NTC: the ELEMENT produces heat; the NTC only SENSES it. Dead-cold on a genuine hot wash => element; implausible/incorrect/intermittent temperature or wrong progression with a serviceable heater => NTC. Do not assume a universal NTC resistance value - it is component/model specific.

SEQUENCE: don't diagnose the heating system just because the water isn't hot if the machine hasn't reached the heating stage - inadequate fill / water level / early abort can be upstream (see inlet-valve / pressure-switch).

HEATER BRACKET [front-entry designs only]: a physically damaged heater (contacted the drum, mechanical noise, repeated failures) means inspect the retaining support/bracket to find why - don't just fit another heater.

HOT/COLD-FILL [older architecture only]: separate hot+cold inlets can mask a failed internal heater on warmer cycles, so intermittent progression does not exclude the heater. Not applicable to cold-fill-only machines.
SAFETY: serious burning smell, melted insulation or smoke at the heater/terminals => stop-use, not continued operation.
adviceBeforeReplacement: establish it should genuinely be heating (programme/temperature; not just cold rinses) before suspecting the heater
confirm it fills to the correct level and actually reaches the heating stage
on a front-entry-heater design with a physically damaged heater, inspect the heater support/bracket and find why it was damaged
if there is a serious burning smell, melted insulation or smoke, stop using the machine
washing-machine:heater.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): a serious burning smell, melted insulation or smoke at the heater/terminals means stop using the machine - do not keep running it to reproduce the fault.
washing-machine:heater.clarifyingQuestion: What makes you think it isn't heating - does the programme finish normally but the washing seems cold, or does it stop / take much longer / show an error?
washing-machine:heater.secondaryQuestion: What temperature and programme are you using, and does the machine have both a hot and a cold water inlet or only a cold one?

on a multi-way valve one fill path works and another does not
against: inadequate supply before the valve
blocked inlet mesh or kinked hose
the programme hasn't reached the fill stage
the door hasn't locked where the machine requires confirmed locking before fill

components.name: pressure system / water-level sensing
supports: machine behaves as though water is already present
abnormal level behaviour / strange fill-drain sequencing
against: obvious supply restriction / blocked mesh / confirmed valve fault
door hasn't locked or programme hasn't progressed

components.name: control PCB / wiring to the valve
supports: supply, inlet path and valve all shown good

against: simpler supply/hydraulic/sequencing causes not yet excluded

commonConfusion.name: door lock / start sequencing (not a fill fault)
commonConfusion.note: Many machines will not begin filling until the control has confirmed the door is safely locked. 'I press start and no water comes in' can be a door-lock/sequencing issue, not a fill-system failure. Establish whether the machine has actually reached the fill stage first (see door-lock).
wouldApplyIf: the door doesn't lock / no lock click
programme doesn't progress into the cycle
a door-related error

commonConfusion.name: inlet valve (as the automatic answer to 'no fill')
commonConfusion.note: 'No fill' does NOT mean a failed inlet valve. Exclude property supply, isolation tap, kinked hose, blocked inlet mesh and door-lock/sequencing before recommending the valve.
wouldApplyIf: supply good AND tap open AND hose clear AND mesh clear AND door locks AND programme reaches fill, but no water passes

commonConfusion.name: control PCB (as a generic fallback)
commonConfusion.note: Do not use PCB/wiring as the default for 'won't fill'. Keep it low until external supply, sequencing, inlet path and the valve are shown good.
wouldApplyIf: valve shown capable of operating but not energised when fill is commanded, with wiring/connector evidence

discriminators: SPLIT THE COMPLAINT FIRST: no fill vs slow/insufficient fill vs genuine overfill vs continuous filling with the level not rising - these need different reasoning, not one static component order.

NO FILL: establish external supply FIRST - are the other cold taps in the property normal? If other taps are affected, strongly down-rank an appliance part. Then tap open -> hose unkinked -> inlet mesh clear -> THEN the inlet valve. The machine may also refuse to fill until the door has locked (sequencing), which is not a fill-system failure.

SLOW FILL: move the inlet mesh/filter and supply/pressure checks UP; a gradually worsening trickle with good supply elsewhere is usually a restriction (mesh/hose/tap), not a dead valve. Do NOT encode one manufacturer's flow/pressure threshold as a universal spec.

OVERFILL (level gets too high): use the switched-off test - if water keeps entering with the machine SWITCHED OFF, strongly suspect a mechanically passing/stuck inlet valve; if it stops when off, the level-sensing/pressure path is more likely (see pressure-switch).

CONTINUOUS FILLING BUT LEVEL NOT RISING: if water keeps entering but the level stays low, suspect water leaving at the same time - siphoning from drain-hose installation (often after a move), NOT genuine overfill or the inlet valve. (No dedicated taxonomy node yet - see the Story-10 taxonomy report.)
adviceBeforeReplacement: check the other cold taps in the property before suspecting the appliance
check the appliance isolation tap is fully open
check the fill hose for kinks/crushing (especially after a move) - replace the hose only if it is physically damaged
inspect and clean the inlet mesh/filter
confirm the door locks and the programme actually reaches the fill stage before recommending the inlet valve
washing-machine:inlet-valve.clarifyingQuestion: Does no water come in at all, does it fill very slowly, or does it keep filling until the water level gets too high?
washing-machine:inlet-valve.secondaryQuestion: Are the other cold taps in the property working normally, and does the door lock when you start the programme?

washing-machine:pressure-switch._approved: Story 10 — engineer-reviewed OVERFILL / water-level-sensing path. Treats the pressure sensing path as a SYSTEM (chamber/hose/sensor); hard-water residue is supporting environmental evidence only.

components.name: inlet valve mechanically stuck open / passing
supports: water continues entering while the machine is SWITCHED OFF
filling continues with no active programme
water gradually appears in the drum while idle
against: water stops immediately when the control stops requesting fill
overfill only occurs during active programme control (points to level sensing)

components.name: pressure chamber / small-bore pressure hose (sensing path)
supports: overfills while powered/running but the inlet valve closes when switched off
restriction/contamination in the pressure path
pressure hose blocked, kinked, split, disconnected or leaking
hard-water area/history with genuine overfill (supporting evidence)
against: inlet valve keeps passing water with the machine switched off

components.name: pressure switch / electronic level sensor
supports: pressure chamber and hose confirmed clear/intact
overfill only while the machine is actively controlling fill
level-sensor error, with the valve closing correctly when the command is removed
against: pressure chamber/hose restriction still plausible

components.name: wiring / control PCB
supports: inlet valve sound AND pressure path sound AND sensor verified
incorrect electrical command to the valve
wiring/connector evidence
against: simpler valve or pressure-system explanations remain

commonConfusion.name: pressure switch (as the automatic answer to overfill)
commonConfusion.note: Overfill does NOT automatically mean a failed pressure switch. The pressure chamber and small-bore pressure hose can stop correct level information reaching an otherwise-good sensor. Treat the sensing path as a system: chamber contamination -> hose restriction -> hose damage/leak/disconnection -> sensor -> wiring.
wouldApplyIf: genuine overfill, inlet valve closes when switched off, and the pressure chamber/hose is confirmed clear and intact

commonConfusion.name: genuine overfilling (vs siphoning)
commonConfusion.note: 'Keeps filling' is not always overfilling. If water enters continuously but the LEVEL does not rise, water may be siphoning away (drain-hose installation, often after a move) - not an overfill/level-sensing fault.
wouldApplyIf: the water level actually rises too high (not merely continuous entry with a low level)

discriminators: SWITCHED-OFF TEST is the highest-value overfill discriminator: water still entering with the machine OFF = mechanically passing/stuck inlet valve; entry stops when OFF = level-sensing/pressure path (chamber/hose/sensor).

Treat the pressure sensing path as a SYSTEM - do NOT jump straight to 'replace the pressure switch'. Check the pressure chamber and small-bore hose (contamination/restriction/damage/disconnection) before condemning the sensor.

HARD-WATER (environmental, supporting evidence ONLY): in hard-water areas limescale residue in the pressure chamber or small-bore pressure hose can block the rising-level signal. A hard-water area + genuine overfill (valve closes when off) increases suspicion of the pressure PATH - but location alone does NOT diagnose a pressure-system fault, and do not assume/fabricate the local water hardness.
LEVEL NOT RISING despite continuous entry = siphoning/drain-hose installation, not overfill (see inlet-valve continuous-fill note and the taxonomy report).
adviceBeforeReplacement: do the switched-off test (does water keep entering with the machine off?) before choosing between the valve and the sensing path
check/clean the pressure chamber and the small-bore pressure hose - especially in hard-water areas
check the pressure hose isn't split, blocked, kinked or disconnected before replacing the pressure switch/level sensor
washing-machine:pressure-switch.clarifyingQuestion: Does water keep coming into the machine even when it's switched off?
washing-machine:pressure-switch.secondaryQuestion: Is the water level actually getting too high, or does it keep taking water without the level rising much?

washing-machine:leak-flood._approved: Story 13 — engineer-reviewed LEAK assessment. Diagnose by WHERE + WHEN + water APPEARANCE, not 'leak -> part'. Causal chains: the leaking component may be the victim, not the cause. Left/right layout is conditional field evidence, NOT universal. CHECK vs PART preserved.

components.name: leak location / cycle stage / water appearance (establish first)
supports: complaint is just 'it's leaking' / 'water underneath' with no location or timing
against: WHERE (front/back/underneath), WHEN (fill/wash/drain-spin) and appearance (clean/soapy/oily) are already known
