supports: water backs up out of the soap drawer or runs down the front from the dispenser DURING FILL
detergent/softener/limescale residue or blocked channels
lots of foam / suds around drawer or door
too much or unsuitable detergent
against: leak is at the door, underneath, or during drain/spin
dispenser path and drawer are clean and clear

components.name: dispenser-to-tub hose
supports: leaks DURING FILL and appears underneath on the LEFT (viewed from front) WHERE THE ARCHITECTURE PUTS THE DISPENSER PATH THERE
split/displaced hose or loose connection on the fill-to-tub path
machine NOT moved but internal fill leak on one side
against: direct evidence the layout differs on this model
leak clearly at rear fill connection / door / pump

components.name: external fill hose / rear connection
supports: leak visibly at the rear connection/hose
machine recently moved/installed/disconnected
damaged hose/washer visible
starts when mains pressure applied
against: not moved/disturbed and leak originates inside the cabinet (uncommon as a spontaneous new fault otherwise)

components.name: door seal (boot)
supports: water visibly passes through the seal
visible tear/split/hole or a foreign object has punctured it
leak correlates with water reaching the damaged area
against: water is running down from the dispenser above
source is the filter/pump area or underneath/rear
oversudsing is the real escape mechanism
seal fold just dirty/gunged (clean first)

components.name: sump / tub-to-pump hose
supports: leak from underneath/centre once the tub HOLDS water (during wash), external hoses dry
split/displaced hose, loose clip, or foreign-object damage
door and dispenser excluded
against: leak only during incoming fill
leak only while the pump is discharging
clear door-seal source

components.name: filter cap / filter housing seating
supports: started leaking AFTER cleaning the filter
cap not fully seated / cross-threaded
debris on the sealing face or damaged filter seal
against: never touched the filter and the pump body/housing itself is cracked/leaking

components.name: drain pump / pump housing
supports: leak correlates strongly with PUMP OPERATION (draining/spin), relatively CLEAN water, appears underneath on the RIGHT (viewed from front) WHERE ARCHITECTURE PUTS THE PUMP THERE
cracked pump/filter housing or pump body/seal leaking, connections sound
against: filter cap incorrectly refitted (check first)
drain hose/waste connection leaking
leak occurs before the pump operates
dirty/oily water with bearing noise (bearings)

components.name: drain hose / household waste connection
supports: leak at the drain hose or the sink/standpipe/waste connection
recent install / hose pushed too far or loose
against: leak from the pump body itself
leak before pumping

components.name: drum bearings / tub seal
supports: DIRTY/OILY/GREASY/RUSTY-looking water underneath spreading across the front
combined with rumbling/grinding noise, drum play, or a dropped/off-centre drum, worse on spin
against: clean incoming water or normal soapy wash water
quiet machine with a clear pump/hose/seal source

components.name: loose counterweight / damaged (cracked) tub
supports: a sudden MAJOR leak together with loud banging/impact noise and severe vibration
visible tub damage / loose or broken counterweight
leak far larger than hose seepage
against: small seepage with no abnormal noise
clear minor hose/seal source

components.name: inlet valve passing / overfill route [water while OFF or level too high]
supports: CLEAN water continues ENTERING while the machine is switched OFF (mechanically passing inlet valve - see Story-10)
water level goes abnormally HIGH and THEN water escapes (overfill route - see pressure-switch/inlet-valve)
against: DIRTY waste water appears while off (waste plumbing/backflow, not an appliance part)
normal level with a plain hose/seal leak

commonConfusion.name: the leaking component is the failed component
commonConfusion.note: Often the component water escapes through is the VICTIM, not the cause. A ripped door seal can be caused by a dropped drum/bearing; a cracked tub by a loose counterweight; an escape point by an overfill or oversudsing event. Ask WHY it leaked.
wouldApplyIf: there is supporting evidence of an underlying mechanical/level/dosing cause

commonConfusion.name: door seal ripped = just replace the seal
commonConfusion.note: If the boot is badly ripped, check for abnormal drum play / a dropped drum / bearing noise first - a rotating drum contacting the seal tears it, and a new seal will be destroyed too if the drum fault isn't fixed.
wouldApplyIf: seal torn AND drum has up/down play, sits low, or rumbles on spin

commonConfusion.name: water at the front = door seal
commonConfusion.note: It can equally be the dispenser above (down the front), the filter/pump area, or oversudsing. Locate the true source first.
wouldApplyIf: water is clearly seen passing THROUGH the door seal, not from above or below

commonConfusion.name: foam coming out = a failed seal/pump
commonConfusion.note: Excessive foam (too much/unsuitable detergent) can push water/foam out of the drawer/door/vent with NO failed part. Check dosing/oversudsing first.
wouldApplyIf: a genuine leak persists with correct detergent and no excess foam

commonConfusion.name: leaks during fill = external inlet hose
commonConfusion.note: A fill hose spontaneously leaking is relatively uncommon unless the machine was recently moved/disturbed or is visibly damaged. During fill, also strongly consider the dispenser path and dispenser-to-tub hose.
wouldApplyIf: leak clearly at the rear connection, or the machine was recently moved/reconnected

commonConfusion.name: large leak = split hose
commonConfusion.note: A big leak WITH severe mechanical banging can be a loose counterweight cracking the tub - not a simple hose.
wouldApplyIf: large sudden leak accompanied by loud banging / severe vibration

commonConfusion.name: foam from the drawer/door = a leak
commonConfusion.note: Excess foam escaping is over-sudsing (foam-suds), not a hydraulic leak — the escape point is a consequence. Clear or dirty WATER escaping is a real leak.
wouldApplyIf: actual water (not foam) is escaping the machine

discriminators: COMMIT-FIRST: an explicit report of external water pooling/escaping - 'leaking underneath', 'water/puddle on the floor', 'leaks water', 'water pouring out' - is enough on its own to COMMIT the leak-flood route; do not withhold the route or ask whether it is really a leak. (Water specifically from the DETERGENT DRAWER/soap dispenser still belongs to the dispenser route, not generic leak-flood.) THEN DIAGNOSE BY WHERE + WHEN + APPEARANCE: location (front/back/underneath, left/right), cycle stage (fill / wash / drain-spin / while off), and water appearance (clean / soapy-dirty / oily-dirty) pin the part far better than 'leak' alone. Use these ONLY to narrow the source component (door seal, sump hose, drain pump, dispenser, inlet valve, tub/bearing) as a follow-up refinement - not as a precondition for routing.
DURING FILL: dispenser path first (drawer residue/oversudsing = CHECK), then dispenser-to-tub hose; external rear fill hose rises mainly after a recent move/disturbance or visible damage.
LEFT SIDE + DURING FILL => strongly consider the dispenser-to-tub hose/path WHERE THE MODEL LAYOUT SUPPORTS IT - not a universal rule; use the actual architecture if known.

DRAIN/SPIN + RIGHT SIDE + relatively CLEAN water => pump/pump-housing/filter area rises WHERE THE MODEL LAYOUT SUPPORTS IT - again not universal. But if it started after a filter clean, check the filter cap/seal seating BEFORE the pump.
DIRTY/OILY water underneath across the front + rumbling/drum play/dropped drum => drum bearings / tub seal (a multi-observation call, not 'water underneath = pump').
BIG sudden leak + loud banging/impact => loose counterweight cracking the tub; don't reduce to 'split hose'.
WHILE OFF: CLEAN water still ENTERING => mechanically passing inlet valve (Story-10); DIRTY water backing in => waste plumbing/backflow, not an appliance part.

OVERFILL masquerade: if the water level goes abnormally high and THEN it leaks, diagnose the overfill cause (pressure chamber/hose/level sensing/passing valve) - the escape point may be a consequence, not the fault.

CAUSAL CHAINS: (A) bearing/drum-drop -> seal ripped; (B) loose counterweight -> tub cracked; (C) overfill -> secondary escape; (D) oversudsing -> foam escapes. Address the underlying cause, not just the escape point.
SAFETY: a large uncontrolled leak or water reaching electrical parts is a stop-use situation, not continued operation.
adviceBeforeReplacement: establish WHERE the water appears, WHEN in the cycle, and what it LOOKS like before choosing a part
if it started after cleaning the filter, re-seat the filter cap/seal and check the sealing face before suspecting the pump
if water comes from the drawer during fill, check for detergent/softener residue, a blocked dispenser and oversudsing (dosing) first
if the door seal is ripped, check the drum for up/down play, a dropped drum or bearing noise so a replacement seal isn't destroyed too
if the leak is at the rear, check whether the machine was recently moved and the fill-hose connection/washer
if there is a big leak with heavy banging, check for a loose counterweight / cracked tub
washing-machine:leak-flood.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): a large uncontrolled leak, or water reaching electrical parts, means stop using the machine and isolate it rather than continuing to run it.
washing-machine:leak-flood.clarifyingQuestion: Where does the water seem to come from - front, back or underneath - and does it start while filling, washing, or draining/spinning?
washing-machine:leak-flood.secondaryQuestion: Is the leaking water clean, soapy/dirty wash water, or dirty/oily-looking water?

discriminators: COMMIT-FIRST: an explicit report of external water pooling/escaping - 'leaking underneath', 'water/puddle on the floor', 'leaks water', 'water pouring out' - is enough on its own to COMMIT the leak-flood route; do not withhold the route or ask whether it is really a leak. (Water specifically from the DETERGENT DRAWER/soap dispenser still belongs to the dispenser route, not generic leak-flood.) THEN pin the source part by WHERE it leaks from and WHAT the water looks like - that pins the part far better than the word 'leak' alone. Use location + timing + water appearance ONLY to narrow the source component (door seal, sump hose, drain pump, dispenser, inlet valve, tub/bearing) as a follow-up refinement - not as a precondition for routing.

Leaking DOWN THE FRONT from the DETERGENT DRAWER = a blocked / gunged-up detergent dispenser: soap and softener build up and the incoming water backs up out of the drawer. Fix = clean the dispenser/drawer. Not a pump or seal.

Leaking FROM THE DOOR = the DOOR SEAL (boot). GOTCHA: many door-seal leaks are just a DIRTY/gunged seal fold or debris trapped across it (coin, wire, fabric) - clean the seal fold and clear debris FIRST; only replace the boot if it's actually split or perished.

Leaking ON SPIN or WHILE EMPTYING/DRAINING with CLEAN water = the DRAIN PUMP (or the sump hose to it): under drain/spin the pump is pressurised, so a cracked pump body, worn pump seal or split sump hose pushes clean water out. Top suspect for spin/empty leaks.

Leaking DIRTY water, especially with a NOISY / rumbling drum = worn DRUM BEARINGS / failed tub seal: water gets past the tub seal (so it looks dirty) and the bearings are failing. Dirty-water leak plus noise = bearings, not the pump.
washer-dryer:leak-flood.clarifyingQuestion: Where does the water come from - down the front by the drawer, at the door, or underneath on spin - and is it clean or dirty?

belt-driven architecture
pulley loose/cracked where inspected
against: DIRECT-DRIVE architecture (no pulley) - do NOT recommend

commonConfusion.name: banging on spin = shock absorbers
commonConfusion.note: Check LOAD and INSTALLATION first. Uneven/too-full/too-small loads and unremoved transit bolts / an unlevel machine cause far more 'banging on spin' than failed dampers.
wouldApplyIf: excessive tub bounce across NORMAL balanced loads, level, transit restraints excluded

commonConfusion.name: brand-new machine shaking violently = faulty suspension
commonConfusion.note: Not until transit brackets/bolts and levelling are checked - forgotten transit bolts are the classic cause of a new/just-moved machine jumping about.
wouldApplyIf: transit bolts confirmed removed and machine level, yet still unstable on balanced loads

commonConfusion.name: noisy spin = bearings
commonConfusion.note: Too broad - characterise the noise. Deep rumble/roar+play = bearings; heavy solid knock = counterweight; light tick once per rev = paddle/foreign object; deeper rhythmic tick = pulley/belt (belt-driven).
wouldApplyIf: a deep grumbling/rumbling that worsens with speed, with drum play

commonConfusion.name: dropped drum = bearings
commonConfusion.note: Incomplete - the drum spider/support can also cause a dropped/wobbly drum. Bearing and spider are related but distinct candidates.
wouldApplyIf: up/down play with a bearing rumble (bearing) vs off-centre wobble beyond simple play (spider)

commonConfusion.name: ticking = bearings
commonConfusion.note: A tick is not a bearing failure without bearing evidence - consider a broken paddle, a foreign object between the tubs, or (deeper rhythmic) the pulley/belt.
wouldApplyIf: a deep continuous rumble, not a discrete tick

commonConfusion.name: large leak after violent banging = a hose
commonConfusion.note: A big leak WITH heavy banging can be a loose counterweight that has cracked the tub - address the mechanical cause, not just the escape point (Story-13/14 chain).
wouldApplyIf: large sudden leak with severe banging/instability

discriminators: NOISE IS NOT ONE SYMPTOM - route by CHARACTER: violent banging/shaking => load/installation/transit first, then counterweight/suspension; heavy SOLID knock => counterweight/major suspension; deep GRUMBLING/RUMBLING/ROARING (worse with speed) + play => drum bearing (seal/support); LIGHT metallic tick/scrape once per rev => paddle or foreign object between tubs; DEEPER rhythmic tick/knock => pulley or worn belt (belt-driven only). Combine with timing/load/architecture, not as absolute acoustic labels.
NEW / RECENTLY MOVED + violent vibration => TRANSIT bolts/brackets + levelling FIRST; do not recommend suspension parts until excluded.
LOAD-SPECIFIC (bath mat/duvet/single heavy/very small/overloaded) => unbalanced-load CHECK (Story 11), not suspension/bearing parts. Fine with an ordinary load confirms this.
WALKS ACROSS THE FLOOR => level/feet/floor and stationary-rock check before parts.
BEARING + OILY MARKS ON CLOTHING (or dirty/oily leak) => drum bearing/seal is strong combined evidence (cross-ref Story-13).
DROPPED/WOBBLY DRUM => bearing AND drum spider/support are both candidates - don't collapse every dropped drum into 'bearings'.
ARCHITECTURE: offer drum pulley / drive belt only on belt-driven machines; on direct-drive there is neither (Story 11).
CAUSAL CHAINS: bearing/spider -> drum play/drop -> door seal ripped -> leak (Story 13); loose counterweight -> banging -> tub cracked -> major leak (Story 13/14). Address the underlying cause.
RETAINED WATER + won't spin (banging while trying to spin with water still in the drum) => drainage remains authoritative (Story 9), not vibration.
SAFETY: a big leak with violent banging, or a machine moving dangerously, is a stop-use situation, not continued operation.

DROPPED / WOBBLING DRUM that also catches or marks clothes = worn bearing / broken suspension (this fault or motor-drum), NOT damaging-clothes: the fabric damage is a CONSEQUENCE of the mechanical play, so fix the mechanical fault. A LOOSE paddle that rattles/knocks with movement is mechanical here; only a BROKEN paddle with a sharp edge that snags fabric (no drum movement) is damaging-clothes.
adviceBeforeReplacement: establish the noise CHARACTER (bang/knock/rumble/tick/scrape), whether it moves, and whether it's load-specific before choosing a part
on a new or recently-moved machine, check the transit bolts/brackets are removed and the machine is level with feet locked
try an ordinary evenly-distributed load to rule out load imbalance
with the power off, rotate the drum by hand for roughness/rumble and check for up/down play (bearing) or off-centre wobble (spider)
if there's a big leak with heavy banging, check for a loose counterweight / cracked tub

commonConfusion.name: burning smell / older machine = PCB or automatic carbon brushes
commonConfusion.note: On a confirmed BRUSHED motor, severely worn carbon brushes cause sparking, a burning/electrical smell and intermittent operation - so brushes rise there. But don't assume brushes on a brushless motor, and don't default to the PCB. Significant burning/smoke means stop-use first (see safety).
wouldApplyIf: confirmed brushed motor with sparking/burning-smell and intermittent rotation

commonConfusion.name: repeated slow drum movements / violent abort = failing motor
commonConfusion.note: Slow back-and-forth is deliberate load redistribution (drive works). Accelerate-then-violent-bang-then-abort is imbalance/levelling/suspension. Neither is automatically a motor fault.
wouldApplyIf: drum never turns at all, or the same failure repeats with a sensible balanced load

commonConfusion.name: clothes too wet / poor spin = motor or brushes
commonConfusion.note: Poor-spin is a ROUTER: rule out retained water (not-draining), load imbalance (unbalanced-load), spin-speed/programme selection, and excessive foam (foam-suds) BEFORE motor/brushes/tacho. Slow back-and-forth redistribution means the drive works.
wouldApplyIf: the drum drains fully, the load is balanced and full-spin is selected, yet it still won't reach spin speed

commonConfusion.name: direct-drive won't spin = motor/brushes
commonConfusion.note: On a direct-drive/brushless machine there are NO carbon brushes and NO belt; abnormal powered movement with a free drum points to hall/rotor-position sensing or the inverter (see hall-sensor), after ruling out retained water/imbalance/jam.
wouldApplyIf: confirmed direct-drive, drum free by hand, abnormal powered twitching

discriminators: MODE SPLIT FIRST: (A) wash tumble works and only the FAST SPIN fails => spin-management: retained water (drainage), unbalanced load, overload, or reduced/no-spin programme - not a dead motor. (B) drum NEVER turns in wash or spin => genuine drive/drum fault.

PHYSICAL HAND-TURN (power off): drum STIFF/JAMMED/part-rotation => mechanical (foreign object / bearings / seizure) rises before any electronics. Drum turns FREELY => drive system (belt/brushes/capacitor/motor per architecture).
MOTOR HEARD, DRUM STATIONARY: on a belt-driven machine the drive belt/transmission rises sharply; on direct-drive the belt is absent and diagnosis follows the actual drive architecture.

ARCHITECTURE-AWARE (constrain candidates by the model where known): offer a DRIVE BELT only on belt-driven machines; CARBON BRUSHES only on brushed universal motors; a START/RUN CAPACITOR only on capacitor-start motors. Do not recommend a part the architecture doesn't have.
RETAINED WATER: no-spin with water left in the drum is a drainage route (see not-draining), NOT the motor. Empty drum => continue spin/drive diagnosis.

Existing engineer noise guide: deep RUMBLING/grinding worsening on spin = worn DRUM BEARINGS (rock the inner drum for up/down play); TICKING/knocking with paddles snapping = a trapped FOREIGN OBJECT; WHIPPING/slapping = a worn DRIVE BELT; the drain pump is the LAST suspect for noise.

CLOTHES DAMAGE + MECHANICAL EVIDENCE: if clothes are marked/caught/torn AND the drum has dropped/sagged, wobbles, or rumbles/roars on spin, the ROOT CAUSE is the worn drum bearing/spider (motor-drum) — the dropped drum fouls the seal/cabinet. GREASY or BLACK/OILY marks on washing = bearing grease driven past the tub seal. Ground motor-drum (or excessive-vibration when noise/instability dominates), NOT damaging-clothes.
adviceBeforeReplacement: confirm all the water has drained before treating it as a spin fault
try a normal, evenly-distributed load (and check the spin/programme setting isn't reduced/off)
with the power off, turn the drum by hand to tell mechanical (stiff) from drive (free)
identify the drive architecture (belt-driven vs direct-drive; brushed vs brushless; capacitor-equipped) before recommending a drive part
if there is significant burning smell, smoke or heavy sparking, stop using the machine and do not keep power-testing it
washing-machine:motor-drum.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): a significant electrical burning smell, smoke or abnormal/excessive sparking means stop using the machine - do not keep running it powered for diagnosis.
washing-machine:motor-drum.clarifyingQuestion: Does the drum turn normally during the wash and only fail on the fast spin, or does it not turn at all?
washing-machine:motor-drum.secondaryQuestion: With the machine switched off does the drum turn freely by hand, and is all the water gone before it tries to spin?

discriminators: Even for a brief 'won't spin at all', COMMIT to this motor/drum fault (usual causes: worn CARBON BRUSHES or the DRIVE BELT) and use the checks to refine - don't withhold a diagnosis. But weigh two things first: (1) WATER - it won't spin until drained, so no-spin with water left is a DRAIN fault (drain pump / blocked filter), not the motor. (2) LOAD - an unbalanced load (bathmat, one heavy item) makes it abort the spin; redistributing fixes it. If neither applies, it's a motor/drive fault (brushes/belt).

Identify the MOTOR TYPE first. A CARBON-BRUSH (universal) motor's speed is controlled by a module fast-switching a triac; no-spin here is usually WORN BRUSHES, and low brushes sparking can blow a MOTOR THERMAL FUSE - so it can be brushes and/or the fuse. Hand-spinning the drum and listening tells you if brushes are worn down.

An INDUCTION motor has NO brushes - it is capacitor-start (a START CAPACITOR gives a start winding ~90 degrees out of phase). No-spin/won't-start on a brushless machine points to the START CAPACITOR or windings, not brushes.
A snapped/slipped DRIVE BELT gives motor-running but drum-not-turning.

NOISY washer-dryer - tell by the KIND of noise: deep RUMBLING/grinding worse on spin = worn DRUM BEARINGS (grip the inner drum, up/down play confirms it). TICKING/knocking, or drum paddles snapping off = a FOREIGN OBJECT trapped (bra wire, coin). WHIPPING/slapping = worn DRIVE BELT. A cracked MOTOR PULLEY on the back of the drum also causes noise. The drain PUMP is rarely noisy - it tends to just jam - so treat the pump as the LAST suspect for a noise complaint.
washer-dryer:motor-drum.clarifyingQuestion: Is there still water in the drum, was it a big/uneven load, and can you hear the motor trying while the drum stays still?

discriminators: CLEAN THE FILTER FIRST (a CHECK, not a part). On vented and condenser dryers the lint/fluff filter (and the condenser filter) is user-cleanable and routinely neglected. A clogged filter restricts airflow, the dryer overheats and TRIPS THE THERMAL CUT-OUT (TOC), which kills the heat - so a blocked filter/vent is the cheapest and most common cause, rule it out before selling parts.

On a VENTED or CONDENSER dryer the STRONG FIRST hardware candidate for genuine no-heat is the heater ELEMENT: dryer heaters are relatively fragile and commonly fail OPEN (simply stop heating). When the element has failed, ALSO check/replace the THERMAL CUT-OUT and thermostat - they are cheap and commonly fail together, and the overheat that opened one often stresses the other. Note: unlike a built-in OVEN, earth-leakage is NOT the dominant dryer-heater failure mode, so do not copy the oven priors - a dryer heater usually just goes open-circuit and cold.

A HEAT-PUMP dryer is completely different and has NO conventional heating element - do NOT recommend an element/TOC for it. It dries with a sealed refrigeration circuit (a fridge in reverse). No-heat/not-drying on a heat-pump points to a blocked CONDENSER/EVAPORATOR FILTER first (cheap, common), then the refrigerant/heat-pump circuit or its sensors - a specialist repair. If the architecture is unknown and it changes the answer, establish vented/condenser/heat-pump before recommending a heater part.

NORMAL-BEHAVIOUR BOUNDARY: a heat-pump dryer normally runs at a LOWER drum temperature and a LONGER programme than an old vented dryer. So 'only feels warm rather than very hot' and 'takes longer than my old vented dryer' are usually NORMAL and must NOT by themselves produce a fault/part diagnosis. Reassure and, if anything, suggest cleaning the filters and reducing load.

Ground a hardware fault only on stronger evidence: worsening performance over time, genuinely COLD operation that never dries, abnormal cycle behaviour, error codes, airflow restriction, or sensor/compressor evidence. The cheap common cause of gradually poor drying is a blocked CONDENSER/EVAPORATOR filter (clean first); the sealed refrigerant circuit is a specialist/costly repair and the last resort.

Squeal/chirp or slipping while it still turns = JOCKEY/idler tension pulley or a glazed belt. Motor HUMS but won't turn (drum free by hand) = MOTOR START CAPACITOR, not a dead motor. Only when belt, pulley and capacitor are excluded consider the motor itself.

A genuinely SEIZED drum/bearing is RARE. 'Drum hard to turn by hand' with a rumble/grinding and drum play points to worn support rollers/pads (front) or the rear bearing/bush - not the motor. Do not make seized bearings the default answer to a non-turning drum.

discriminators: Overheating and a tripped thermal cut-out are usually the EFFECT of restricted airflow, not the root cause. Work the causal order: fluff/lint filter, then the air path/vent, then the condenser/heat exchanger where fitted, then the BLOWER FAN operating, then the heater/thermostat control - and only THEN the TOC itself. Replacing a TOC without fixing the airflow leaves the real fault in place and it will trip again.
So 'I changed the thermal cutout and it has gone again' is a classic airflow/fan problem - investigate the filter, fan and air path, do not just fit another TOC.

A strong burning-LINT smell, smoke, scorching or repeated severe overheating is a FIRE RISK: STOP USING the dryer, unplug it at the wall, and do not run another cycle 'to see if it happens again'. Clean out the lint safely and get it checked; do not attempt live mains testing.

discriminators: Route dryer noise by CHARACTER; do not encode 'noisy = motor' or 'noisy = bearing'. SQUEAL/CHIRP with the drum still turning -> jockey/idler tension pulley or a glazed belt (consider these before a motor or a seized drum). RHYTHMIC THUMP -> drum support roller, a belt joint, or the load. SCRAPING -> drum support/felt or a foreign object. RATTLE (especially as the fan starts) -> blower fan or a loose object. HUM with NO drum movement -> motor/start capacitor or a mechanical jam (see drum-drive). An unusual COMPRESSOR/refrigeration noise belongs to the heat-pump circuit.
So 'squeals but the drum still turns' should strongly raise the jockey/idler pulley and belt/tension system - NOT the PCB and NOT a seized drum.

Tripping the INSTANT you switch on (before heating) points more to the mains wiring/suppressor or the motor/pump than the element.

On a confirmed HEAT-PUMP dryer there is no conventional element - trips that follow the COMPRESSOR starting point to the compressor/inverter drive electronics, wiring or motor/fans. Do not recommend a conventional heater element for a heat-pump machine.

discriminators: Route by the damage type/evidence - do NOT default to the heater or motor. Most commonly a worn drum FELT/rear SEAL lets small items slip into a gap and catch, or a rough spot/crack/sharp edge on the drum snags fabric. Also check for a trapped foreign object (coin, bra underwire). Scorching/melting rather than tearing points to excessive heat (see overheating), not a mechanical snag.

washer-dryer:drying-heater._approved: WD audit v1 — WON'T-DRY is a differentiated finding, NOT automatically the drying heater. Rule out water-not-removed (poor spin/drain), restricted airflow/condenser, and an over-large dry load first. HOT-but-wet / slow = airflow/condensation; NO heat at all = drying element/thermostat/thermal-cutout (often tripped by airflow restriction). Washer-dryer specific.
likelyComponents: thermal cut-out (may be tripped by airflow restriction)
symptoms: washes fine but clothes not drying
gets hot but clothes stay wet
dries small loads but not a big one
discriminators: WON'T DRY is NOT automatically the drying heater - differentiate first. (1) WATER ACTUALLY REMOVED? If the wash didn't SPIN/DRAIN properly the clothes start the dry soaking and never dry - that is a SPIN / DRAIN / unbalanced-load fault (see not-draining / unbalanced-load / motor-drum), NOT the drying heater. (2) HOT BUT STILL WET, or drying takes far too long, points to restricted AIRFLOW / CONDENSATION - a blocked lint FILTER or CONDENSER (and, on condenser designs that use cooling water, the water supply) - clean those FIRST, not the heater. (3) NO HEAT AT ALL (drum turns, air stays cold) points to the drying HEATER ELEMENT, its THERMOSTAT, or a tripped THERMAL CUT-OUT. (4) TOO BIG A DRY LOAD dries poorly with no fault at all.

THERMAL CUT-OUT gotcha: a tripped drying thermal cut-out is usually the SYMPTOM of earlier airflow restriction (blocked filter/condenser), not a random failure - clean the airflow path and look for a reset before condemning parts.

A washer-dryer dries a SMALLER load than it washes - a full wash load put straight onto dry, or an overloaded drum, gives poor drying with no failed part. Suggest a smaller dry load before replacing anything.

A BURNING / HOT / SCORCHING smell while DRYING is normally FLUFF & LINT scorching on the hot drying ELEMENT because airflow is restricted - clean the lint FILTER (and check the vent/condenser) FIRST; if the smell is strong, unplug it and let it cool. This is a drying-heater / airflow issue, NOT the cooling fan and NOT the wash side.

If airflow, spin/drain and load are all fine and it still won't heat or smells hot, suspect the drying HEATER ELEMENT or its THERMOSTAT / thermal cut-out. Route a burning-smell-on-dry to the drying heater/overheat side, not to a 'cooling' error.

commonConfusion.name: won't dry / wet clothes = the drying heater
commonConfusion.note: Wet clothes after a dry cycle are NOT automatically a drying-heater fault. Rule out (a) water not removed by a poor spin/drain, (b) restricted airflow/condenser (hot-but-wet or slow drying), and (c) too large a dry load, before the drying element/thermostat. Only NO heat at all with airflow/spin/load fine points to the heater.
wouldApplyIf: the clothes were properly spun (not dripping) before drying, the lint filter/condenser are clean, the dry load is modest, and there is still NO heat during drying

commonConfusion.name: hot but still wet = the heater
commonConfusion.note: If it clearly gets HOT but clothes stay damp (or drying is very slow), the heater is working - the problem is AIRFLOW / CONDENSATION (blocked filter/condenser), not the heating element.
wouldApplyIf: it gets hot during drying yet clothes remain wet, or drying takes far longer than normal

adviceBeforeReplacement: clean the lint/fluff filter and (on condenser models) the condenser, and make sure the airflow path isn't restricted
check the wash actually SPUN and DRAINED the water out - clothes that go into the dry soaking will never dry (that's a wash-side fault)
try a SMALLER dry load - a washer-dryer dries less than it washes
if there is a strong burning smell, stop and unplug it to let it cool before anything else

commonConfusion.name: [S24] gradual poor wash = several failed parts
commonConfusion.note: Hard-water area + gradually slower fill + weakening spray + worsening wash is more likely ONE progressively restricted water path (scale) than the valve, pump and both arms all failing at once. Consider a common restriction before a multi-part diagnosis.
wouldApplyIf: a hard-water area with several gradually-worsening water symptoms

discriminators: Even for a vague 'not cleaning properly', COMMIT to this poor-cleaning fault with the BLOCKED FILTER as the lead cause (by far the most common) and ask what residue is left to refine - don't withhold a diagnosis.

Diagnose a poor-wash by the RESIDUE and rank by likelihood. GRITTY/SANDY residue (like coffee grounds) = a BLOCKED FILTER recirculating dirty water - by far the most common (~60%). Twist out and rinse the bottom filter first.

GREASY/FILMY dishes that are still WET with NO steam/heat right after the cycle = genuine no-heat (heater/flow-through assembly) - next most common (~20%). But wet dishes that are HOT is drying (rinse aid), not heating.
ONE rack or corner consistently unwashed while the rest is clean = CLOGGED/blocked SPRAY ARMS or an arm not spinning - clear the holes (~15%).

Fills and drains but SILENT during the wash, or a loud continuous hum with no spray = the CIRCULATION/WASH PUMP (jammed impeller - e.g. broken glass - or failed motor) - least common (~5%). If the tub is UNDERFILLED, it's a fill problem starving the arms, not the pump.
A WHITE CHALKY film is hard-water/limescale or empty rinse-aid/salt (maintenance/settings), not a failed part - sort salt/rinse-aid and descale before replacing anything.

[S24] Hard water is EVIDENCE, not proof: a hard-water area PLUS progressive water-path symptoms PLUS visible scale/restriction raises a scale/restriction cause - hard-water location ALONE is never a diagnosis.

[S24] COMMON CAUSE: hard-water area + gradually slower fill + weakening spray + worsening wash is more likely ONE progressively restricted water path (scale) than the inlet valve, circulation pump and both spray arms all failing at once. Ask 'is this several faults or one restricted path?' - do NOT shotgun valve + pump + arms + PCB.

[S24] LOCAL vs SYSTEMIC: one arm / one rack / one group of jets favours a LOCAL spray-arm or distribution restriction; slow fill / low water level / ALL spray weak / whole machine washing poorly favours a COMMON water-delivery, level or circulation restriction. Don't diagnose several failed parts when one restricted water path fits better.

[S24] Keep the boundaries: several unrelated ELECTRICAL symptoms / intermittent controls / behaviour that changes with door position => DOOR LOOM, not scale. Water in the base + drain pump running => anti-flood, FIND THE LEAK, not scale.
adviceBeforeReplacement: twist out and rinse the bottom filter
clear the spray-arm jets and check the arms spin
top up salt and rinse aid and descale for chalky film
check the tub fills to the normal level

Safe visible/mechanical checks with the machine switched off are fine. A burning smell, scorched or exposed wiring, smoke, or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate at the socket/spur.

commonConfusion.note: An activated flood switch almost always means WATER IS IN THE BASE, not that the switch has failed - it is doing its job. Find WHY the base is wet; do not replace the flood switch as the first move.

commonConfusion.name: emptied the base tray = fixed
commonConfusion.note: Draining or drying the base tray clears the protection for a wash or two, but if the underlying leak (pump seal, sump hose, tub, spray arm) is still there the tray refills and it triggers again. Emptying the tray is NOT a repair.
wouldApplyIf: the fault returns after a few washes

commonConfusion.note: A split or misdirected spray arm can fire water at the door and mimic a bad seal - check the spray arm and door alignment before selling a seal.

discriminators: Dishwasher leaks are diagnosed by WHERE the water appears. A leak from the SIDE or EDGE of the DOOR during washing is the classic one: a perished/dirty DOOR SEAL, a MISALIGNED/dropped door, or a SPLIT SPRAY ARM firing water at the door - check seal, alignment and spray arm before replacing anything.

Most dishwashers have a base tray with a float / anti-flood (Aquastop) switch that catches INTERNAL leaks (sump hose, pump seals, spray-arm feed, tub). An internal leak often shows as the machine STOPPING / anti-flood triggered / a leak error with NO water on the floor, rather than an obvious puddle.

REPAIR TRAP: draining/drying the base tray makes an anti-flood fault look fixed and it may run for a wash or two, but if the underlying leak is still there the tray refills and it triggers again. 'Emptied the tray and it worked' is NOT a repair - the leaking component still needs finding and fixing.

STRONG anti-flood / base-flood pattern: the tub looks EMPTY, the DRAIN PUMP RUNS CONTINUOUSLY and a normal programme won't start or fill => the float in the base has detected water and put the machine into a protective drain/lockout. Establish that the base is wet, then FIND THE LEAK (sump/pump seals, hoses, tub, spray arm, dispenser). The flood switch is responding correctly - it is NOT the fault unless the base is proven dry and the float is stuck.
Do not keep re-running a machine that keeps flooding its base - the leak remains and water damage continues.

clean/inspect the door seal and check the door sits square
check the lower spray arm isn't split
do not keep running a machine that keeps triggering its flood protection

Do not work on live wiring or manipulate the door loom while powered; burning or exposed wiring => STOP USE.

symptoms: fridge not cold but freezer is
discriminators: Even for a bare 'fridge isn't cold / not cooling' with no other detail, COMMIT to this not-cooling fault (lead causes: door seal, thermostat, fan, or on a frost-free model the defrost/airflow) and ask whether the FREEZER is still cold to refine - don't withhold a diagnosis.

KEY PATTERN: a WARM FRIDGE with a still-COLD FREEZER on a frost-free fridge-freezer is almost always an AIRFLOW failure, NOT the thermostat or a low gas charge. Frost-free models have ONE evaporator coil in the freezer that cools both sections, so if the cold air can't move, the freezer stays cold and the fridge goes warm.

Most likely (~70%) it's the DEFROST SYSTEM: the defrost heater, defrost (bi-metal) thermostat or defrost timer/control fails, so frost never clears and builds into a solid block of ice over the evaporator coil that chokes off the airflow. The fan can be spinning perfectly but cannot push air through the ice. Check the defrost components FIRST.
Less commonly it's the EVAPORATOR FAN MOTOR: the fan seizes, burns out, or its blades jam on stray ice, so cold air isn't pushed into the fridge even though the coil isn't fully iced up.

TELL THEM APART (simple checks): (1) Open the freezer and press the door-light switch by hand - if you hear the fan whirr, the fan has power so a DEFROST blockage is likely; dead silence means the fan is dead or jammed by ice. (2) With the freezer shut, feel the fridge supply vent (top-back): fan audible but little/no air = iced-up coils (defrost). (3) Remove the rear freezer panel: a solid snow-packed block of ice = defrost failure; clear/lightly-frosted coils but a stationary fan = fan motor.

JUST MOVED / JUST DELIVERED and not getting cold? This may be nothing wrong at all: if the fridge was transported on its side/flat, compressor oil runs into the cooling pipes. Powering it on too soon traps oil in the capillary tubes, blocks the refrigerant and can permanently burn out the compressor. Advice: if it was laid flat, stand it upright ~24 hours before switching on; if moved upright, wait 2-4 hours. Don't diagnose a fault until it's stood and then had a few hours running.

OVER-DIAGNOSED THERMOSTAT: if the fridge RUNS CONSTANTLY and never gets cold enough, suspect dirty CONDENSER COILS (dusty coils at the back/underneath) or a poor DOOR SEAL rather than the thermostat - the stat is doing its job, it just can't reach temperature.
fridge-freezer:not-cooling.clarifyingQuestion: Is the freezer still cold while the fridge is warm, and is there a thick block of ice on the back wall inside the freezer?

symptoms: block of ice at the back
discriminators: Frost-free defrost failure = frost never clears and builds into a solid block of ice over the evaporator coil, choking the airflow so the fridge goes warm while the freezer stays cold. The three defrost parts to check: the DEFROST HEATER (burns out), the DEFROST (bi-metal) THERMOSTAT (stuck open so the heater never fires), and the DEFROST TIMER/control (never calls a defrost cycle).

Confirming sign: fan audible but no air at the fridge vent, and a snow-packed ice block on the coils behind the rear freezer panel. Manually defrosting (unplug 24-48h) will temporarily restore cooling - but it WILL ice up again within days until the failed defrost part is replaced, so don't treat 'defrosted it and it worked' as the repair.
fridge-freezer:defrost-system.clarifyingQuestion: Behind the rear panel inside the freezer, are the coils a solid block of ice, or fairly clear?

discriminators: The evaporator (internal) FAN pushes cold air from the freezer coil into the fridge. If it seizes, burns out, or its blades jam on stray ice, the fridge goes warm while the coil itself stays relatively clear of a full ice block.

Tell it from a defrost fault: press the freezer door switch - dead silence with CLEAR coils = fan motor; if you hear the fan but no air reaches the fridge and the coils are a block of ice, it's the DEFROST system, not the fan. A fan fouling on ice points back to a defrost problem too.
fridge-freezer:evaporator-fan.clarifyingQuestion: When you press the freezer door switch, do you hear the fan running, and are the coils clear or iced up?

discriminators: A fridge that's warm all over with the compressor CLICKING or HUMMING every few minutes is trying to start but tripping its thermal OVERLOAD because it can't get going. The cheap, common culprit is the START RELAY / overload (a small plastic pack clipped onto the side of the compressor, ~£15) - check this FIRST: if it rattles when gently shaken or smells/looks burnt, replace the relay before ever condemning the compressor.

It's the COMPRESSOR itself (expensive) only when the relay is sound but it still just hums and clicks - i.e. a mechanical seizure - or when the windings test open/short to the frame. Don't jump to a new compressor (or blame the thermostat) on a click alone: the relay is far more often the fix.
Tie-breaker: if a known-good relay still gives only a hum and a click, the compressor is mechanically seized/dead.
fridge-freezer:compressor.clarifyingQuestion: Is there a clicking/humming every few minutes from the black cylinder at the bottom-back, and does the relay on its side rattle or smell burnt?

symptoms: water at the bottom of the fridge
discriminators: Water pooling under the salad/crisper drawers is overwhelmingly a BLOCKED DEFROST DRAIN: the small hole at the base of the rear (wet) wall clogs with food debris, gunk or ice, so defrost condensation can't run out to the evaporation tray and backs up into the cabinet. Clear the drain hole (cotton bud / flexible cleaner) and flush with warm water first.

If the drain is clear or the water returns fast, check the other causes: food/packaging pressed against the rear wet wall (moisture bridges past the channel); a worn/dirty DOOR SEAL letting warm damp air in (excess condensation); the fridge tilted slightly FORWARD (water misses the trough); or the hidden drain tube FROZEN into an ice block lower down even though the top of the hole looks clear.
This is usually a clean/level/seal fix, not a costly part - lead with clearing the drain and checking levelling and the seal.
fridge-freezer:drainage-blocked.clarifyingQuestion: Is the water only under the salad drawers, and have you tried clearing the small drain hole at the bottom of the back wall?

discriminators: Split fridge noise three ways. FAN HITTING ICE = a rapid rhythmic ticking/clicking/buzz (like a card in bike spokes), from inside the freezer (evaporator fan) or bottom-rear (condenser fan). Verify: open the freezer door - if it STOPS, it's the evaporator fan (door switch cuts it); if the blades are fouling ice it points to a defrost problem or a warped blade.

COMPRESSOR noise = a continuous deep low hum/drone, or a metallic clunk on start/stop, low down at the back. Verify: it changes/stops when you briefly unplug. Cause is wear, perished mounting grommets, or a failing motor.

GENERAL RATTLE / PIPEWORK = an irregular buzzing/rattling that seems to come from everywhere. Verify: press firmly on the panels/back grille/drip tray - if it dampens, it's vibration: fridge not level, copper pipes touching, or a loose drip pan. This is a free fix (level it / separate the pipes / reseat the tray), not a part.
fridge-freezer:noisy.clarifyingQuestion: Does the noise stop when you open the freezer door, when you unplug it briefly, or when you press on the cabinet panels?

discriminators: BEFORE blaming the thermostat, rule out the far more common causes - a thermostat fault is over-diagnosed. Warm fridge + cold freezer = DEFROST system (timer/heater), not the stat. Clicking compressor that won't start = the cheap START RELAY, not the stat. Fresh-food warm while freezer freezes = a stuck AIR DAMPER or the evaporator FAN. Fridge RUNS CONSTANTLY and never shuts off = dirty CONDENSER COILS or a poor DOOR SEAL stopping it reaching temperature (the stat is doing its job) - clean the coils and check the seal first.
Treat it as the thermostat only once those are excluded: e.g. it never calls for cooling at all (stays warm with no compressor run) or won't stop on a mechanical stat with the sensor bulb intact.
fridge-freezer:thermostat.clarifyingQuestion: Is it running constantly and never cold enough (points to coils/seal), or not running at all (points to relay/stat)?

washing-machine:damaging-clothes._approved: Story 19 — engineer-approved (Stage B). Ripping/snagging/marking clothes. Distinguish the TYPE of damage and route to the underlying cause; do not let this node hide a bearing/drum-support/leak failure (D-class #2). CHECK laundry/use before parts.

components.name: laundry / use factors (load, zips, delicates, detergent on delicates)
supports: intermittent, only some items or loads
open zips/hooks or underwired bras washed unbagged
overloaded drum
neat bio detergent or bleach on delicate fabric
damage is random across the load
no unusual noise from the machine
against: the same spot or type of damage every load
damage accompanied by scraping/knocking or a spin rumble
greasy/oily marks together with a bearing rumble

components.name: torn / perished door seal (boot)
supports: front-loader
snags or greasy marks at the door opening
visible split/perish/tear in the rubber
a small water leak at the door too
against: top-loader (no boot seal)
damage originates deep in the drum, not at the opening

components.name: foreign object in the drum or trapped between inner and outer tub
supports: metallic scraping/ticking on tumble or spin
damage started suddenly
small cuts or hard snags (coin, bra underwire, clip, pin)
noise when turning the drum slowly by hand
against: silent operation
fabric snag only, with no cuts

components.name: broken / loose drum paddle (lifter)
supports: rattle/knock inside the drum
a paddle visibly cracked/loose/missing exposing sharp clips
clothes snag on a paddle
against: all paddles secure and intact

components.name: damaged drum surface / burr
supports: a sharp spot felt on the stainless drum
long-term foreign-object abrasion
rust spots or a rough perforation edge
against: drum feels smooth all round by hand

components.name: drum bearing / spider (dropped or rubbing drum)
supports: a deep rumble/grumble on spin AS WELL as the damage
drum has dropped/wobbles and rubs the seal
dirty/oily marks with mechanical noise
against: quiet machine, damage only, no rumble or drop

commonConfusion.name: damaged clothes = replace the door seal
commonConfusion.note: Only if the seal itself is split/perished. A torn seal is often CONSEQUENTIAL to a dropped drum from a failed bearing/spider — fix the mechanical cause, not just the seal.
wouldApplyIf: a visible split in the rubber with no drum rumble or drop

commonConfusion.name: holes in clothes = a machine fault
commonConfusion.note: Often laundry/use: overloading, open zips/underwires, or bio detergent on delicates. Check use before condemning a part.
wouldApplyIf: a consistent mechanical snag point or a trapped sharp object is found

commonConfusion.name: greasy marks + noise = damaging-clothes
commonConfusion.note: Greasy/oily marks with a rumble/grumble on spin is a BEARING/tub-seal failure (see excessive-vibration / leak-flood), not a generic clothes-damage node.
wouldApplyIf: oily marks together with a deep spin rumble or drum play

discriminators: BOUNDARY (Story-18 D-class #2) — decide FIRST: if the report includes ANY mechanical noise (rumble/grumble/grinding/knock on spin), a dropped or wobbly drum, or an oily/greasy leak or oily marks, GROUND the underlying MECHANICAL fault — drum bearing/support (motor-drum or excessive-vibration) or a leak (leak-flood) — NOT damaging-clothes. A ripped seal alongside a dropped/wobbly drum is consequential damage: the bearing/spider/drum-support failure wins.
damaging-clothes is only for PHYSICAL cuts/tears/snags/holes with NO mechanical noise and NO dropped drum: a torn seal lip, a broken paddle, a foreign object, or a drum burr.
Split by TYPE of damage: physical cuts/tears/snags => seal/paddle/foreign-object/burr; greasy/oily marks WITH noise => bearing/tub-seal; white/powder marks => poor-wash-results/dispenser.
Sudden onset + metallic scraping => a foreign object between the tubs (bra wire/coin) or through a drum perforation — inspect before parts.
Same spot/item every wash => a fixed snag: a broken paddle, a burr on the drum, or a split seal lip.
CHECK laundry/use (load size, open zips, underwired bras, bio detergent/bleach on delicates) before recommending any part.

DOWN-RANK GUARD: 'ripped/tearing/holes' ALONE does not make this the fault. If the SAME report has a dropped/sagging/wobbling drum, rumble/roar/grinding on spin, or greasy/black/oily marks, that mechanical fault (motor-drum / excessive-vibration) or a leak (leak-flood) WINS and this is only consequential damage. Choose damaging-clothes ONLY for fabric cuts/snags/holes with NO drum movement and NO mechanical noise: a split seal lip, a sharp broken paddle edge, a foreign object (coin/wire/bra underwire), a drum burr, or a stuck zip.
adviceBeforeReplacement: check pockets and wash bras/delicates in a mesh bag; don't overload the drum
run an empty spin and feel around the drum and inside the seal folds for a sharp spot or a trapped object
if there is also a rumble on spin or the drum drops/wobbles, treat it as a bearing/drum-support fault, not just clothes damage
washing-machine:damaging-clothes.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): unplug before reaching into the drum or seal — burrs, pins and glass shards can cut.
washing-machine:damaging-clothes.clarifyingQuestion: Are the clothes physically cut/torn/snagged (holes, pulls), or coming out marked/greasy but intact — and do you hear any scraping or knocking from the drum?
washing-machine:damaging-clothes.secondaryQuestion: Is it the same spot or type of item every time, or random with heavy or mixed loads?

washing-machine:poor-wash-results._approved: Story 19 — engineer-approved (Stage B). Poor wash / poor rinse / marks-residue. CHECK/advice-first; do not turn poor washing into automatic part sales. Route to heater (no-heat), motor-drum (no agitation), dispenser/foam-suds (delivery/rinse) on real evidence.
symptoms: clothes come out with powder on them

components.name: detergent dose / type and wash habits
supports: white/streaky residue
powder used, especially on cold or short cycles
over-dosing in a low-water HE machine
hard-water area
against: only softener not clearing (=> dispenser/siphon)
clothes physically cut/torn (=> damaging-clothes)

components.name: overloading (poor rinse)
supports: drum packed tight
residue mainly after full loads
clothes have no room to move/rinse
against: happens on small loads too

components.name: programme / temperature selection
supports: a cool/short/eco cycle used for a heavily soiled load
wrong programme for the soiling
against: an appropriate hot programme was already used

components.name: dispenser drawer / siphon not clearing
supports: powder or softener left in the drawer
drawer gunged or blocked
water only trickles into the drawer
against: drawer empties fully but clothes are still marked

components.name: dirty machine — biofilm / limescale
supports: a musty smell as well
gunge/limescale in the door-seal folds
hard-water scale build-up
against: a clean, well-maintained machine

components.name: no heat on hot washes
supports: water stays cold on a hot programme
greasy soiling never shifts (needs heat)
against: the water does get hot

components.name: weak water delivery / poor rinse water
supports: little or no water entering
fill is weak or partial
against: normal fill and water level

commonConfusion.name: poor wash = replace a part
commonConfusion.note: Usually usage: too much or undissolved detergent, too cool a wash, or overloading. Advice first; a part is rare.
wouldApplyIf: genuine no-heat, no drum movement, or no water entering is evidenced

commonConfusion.name: residue on clothes = dispenser fault
commonConfusion.note: If product is left in the DRAWER, that's dispenser; residue on clothes with a clean drawer is dosing/rinse advice.
wouldApplyIf: product is visibly left behind in the drawer

commonConfusion.name: not clean + cold water = poor-wash advice
commonConfusion.note: Genuine no-heat on hot washes is a HEATER/temperature fault (see heater), not detergent advice.
wouldApplyIf: the water never gets hot on a hot programme

discriminators: BOUNDARY — decide FIRST: if the DRUM is not turning/agitating properly GROUND motor-drum; if the water never gets HOT on a hot wash GROUND heater/temperature-sensor; if there is heavy FOAM GROUND foam-suds; if product is left in the DRAWER GROUND dispenser. poor-wash-results is for wash-quality/rinse/residue when the machine otherwise fills, heats, agitates and drains normally.
Mostly CHECK/advice: reduce dose, dissolve powder or use liquid/tablets, don't overload, run an occasional hot maintenance wash, clean the drawer and seal. Rarely a part.
White/powdery residue => undissolved or over-dosed detergent, or hard water. Greasy/grey marks + musty smell => biofilm build-up (maintenance). Product left in the DRAWER => dispenser.
Poor rinse specifically => over-dosing + low water + overloading; cross-link foam-suds, dispenser and inlet-valve where evidence supports.
adviceBeforeReplacement: use less detergent and dissolve powder (or switch to liquid/tablets); don't overload the drum
run an occasional hot (60C+) maintenance wash and clean the drawer and seal folds
if the water never gets hot on a hot wash treat it as a heating fault; if the drum barely turns treat it as a drum/drive fault
washing-machine:poor-wash-results.clarifyingQuestion: Is it a white/powdery residue or greasy streaks, do you use powder or liquid, and how full do you pack the drum?
washing-machine:poor-wash-results.secondaryQuestion: Is there also powder or softener left in the drawer at the end, and does the water get hot on a hot wash?

washing-machine:tacho._approved: Story 19 — engineer-approved (Stage B). Motor speed sensing. Architecture-aware: 'speed error = replace tacho' is NOT acceptable. On brushed motors check carbon brushes first; brushless/direct-drive uses hall/rotor-position (see hall-sensor). Error codes are NOT portable across brands/generations.
symptoms: motor revs up really fast then stops
spins too fast then cuts out
drum spins very fast then stops

components.name: jammed motor / drum
supports: drum stiff or won't turn by hand with the power off
something obstructing the drum
against: drum turns freely and smoothly by hand

components.name: carbon brushes [brushed / universal motor ONLY]
supports: older brushed-motor machine
arcing/sparking or a burning smell from the motor
erratic or over-speed then cut-out
intermittent running or gradual loss of power
against: brushless / inverter / direct-drive motor (no brushes) — do NOT recommend
brushes inspected and still long

components.name: tacho coil / magnet + connector
supports: speed-sensor symptom with brushes proven good (or a brushless machine)
tacho coil open-circuit or dislodged magnet on the motor shaft
no speed feedback / over-speed with a free-turning drum
against: carbon brushes not yet checked on a brushed machine
the drum is mechanically jammed

components.name: wiring / connector motor to control
supports: intermittent speed error
chafed or loose loom to the motor
against: connections sound and secure

components.name: motor speed-sensing electronics / control [architecture-specific]
supports: tacho coil, wiring and brushes all proven good
module/inverter fault indicated by the machine
against: cheaper causes (brushes/coil/wiring) not yet excluded

commonConfusion.name: speed error = replace the tacho
commonConfusion.note: NOT acceptable as a default. On a brushed motor, badly worn carbon brushes cause the same speed-feedback/erratic-speed symptoms — check brushes FIRST where the architecture has them.
wouldApplyIf: brushed motor with brushes inspected and still good, and the coil is open-circuit

commonConfusion.name: error code X = tacho everywhere
commonConfusion.note: Manufacturer error codes are NOT portable across brands/generations, and the same number means different things on brush vs brushless motors — interpret only with make/model context.
wouldApplyIf: make/model is known and its own documentation maps the code to the speed sensor

commonConfusion.name: tacho on a direct-drive machine
commonConfusion.note: Direct-drive/brushless machines have no carbon brushes and use hall/rotor-position sensing instead (see hall-sensor); don't recommend brushes.
wouldApplyIf: a confirmed brushless / direct-drive architecture

discriminators: ARCHITECTURE FIRST: brushed/universal motor => tacho coil + magnet on the shaft AND carbon brushes exist (check brushes before the tacho). Brushless/direct-drive => hall/rotor-position sensing (see hall-sensor), NO brushes.

Distinguish the failure MODE: motor doesn't run at all vs runs intermittently vs over-speeds vs speed hunts vs fails only at high-speed spin vs obvious brush symptoms (arcing/burning). Worn brushes commonly cause intermittent/erratic operation and can trigger speed-sensor error codes.
Error codes are evidence WITH make/model context, NOT universal mappings — do not encode 'code = tacho' across brands.
REPLACEMENT ORDER: rule out a jammed drum (turn by hand) and worn brushes before condemning the tacho coil or the control board.
adviceBeforeReplacement: with the power off, turn the drum by hand to rule out a jam
on an older brushed-motor machine, inspect the carbon brushes before the tacho coil or the board
check the motor loom/connector before replacing any electronics
washing-machine:tacho.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): unplug before inspecting the motor; live motor/PCB testing is for a qualified engineer.
washing-machine:tacho.clarifyingQuestion: Does the motor race/over-speed and then cut out, or fail to build up spin at all — and is it an older machine with a carbon-brush motor?
washing-machine:tacho.secondaryQuestion: Is there an error code, and does the drum turn freely by hand with the machine off?

washing-machine:control-panel._approved: Story 19 — engineer-approved (Stage B). Controls/display misbehaving vs completely dead. True-dead stays low-voltage (supply, lead, mains filter, wiring, PCB last). CHECK control/child lock and a reset first; down-rank the main PCB.
symptoms: wont let me select a programme
screen is blank but it has power
some buttons work and others dont
lights are on but it wont respond

components.name: control lock / child lock engaged
supports: all buttons except power do nothing
a padlock/key symbol is shown
the lock stays on after switching off and on
a lock button was pressed by accident
against: the display is completely dead/blank too (=> power/board)

components.name: power state / reset
supports: a power-cycle at the wall clears a temporary glitch
recently interrupted mid-programme
against: display lit but a physical button is dead (=> panel)

components.name: stuck / dirty button or selector
supports: one control clearly dead while the rest of the UI works
a button physically stuck or a constant beep
a sticky or damaged fascia
against: the whole panel/display is unresponsive

components.name: user-interface / control panel board + ribbon
supports: display blank/partial/garbled but the machine otherwise has power
display segments missing
a moisture- or heat-corroded panel connector
against: the whole machine is completely dead with no lights (=> supply/main PCB)

components.name: communication / wiring panel to main board
supports: display present but not talking to the main board
a communication error shown
against: a single stuck button with the rest working

components.name: main control PCB / supply
supports: UI and wiring proven good
no response with power confirmed to the boards
against: a completely dead machine => supply/low-voltage first (property supply, lead, mains filter, wiring, PCB last)

commonConfusion.name: unresponsive = main PCB
commonConfusion.note: Down-rank the main PCB. Check control-lock, a reset, and a single stuck button / UI board before blaming the main board.
wouldApplyIf: control-lock excluded, a reset tried, and the UI board/ribbon evidenced faulty

commonConfusion.name: dead machine = control panel
commonConfusion.note: A COMPLETELY dead machine (no lights at all) is a SUPPLY/true-dead case (see low-voltage): property supply, lead, mains filter, wiring, PCB last — not the control panel.
wouldApplyIf: display and lights are alive but the controls/display misbehave

commonConfusion.name: buttons dead = faulty panel
commonConfusion.note: Control/child lock is the commonest cause of 'buttons don't work' — check it before a part.
wouldApplyIf: control-lock ruled out and a button is physically stuck or dead

discriminators: FIRST distinguish COMPLETELY DEAD (no lights/display) => low-voltage/supply (true-dead path, PCB last) from POWERED-BUT-MISBEHAVING controls/display => control-panel.
CHECK control/child lock FIRST for 'buttons don't work' (padlock symbol; persists across power-off). Then a power-cycle/reset for a temporary glitch.

One control dead, rest fine => a stuck button/selector or the panel. Whole display blank/garbled but machine powered => UI/control board + ribbon. Display present but not talking to the board => comms/wiring.
Down-rank the main PCB: fascia/control input -> UI/control panel -> communications/wiring -> main PCB, by evidence.
adviceBeforeReplacement: check for a child/control lock (padlock symbol) and turn it off
switch off at the wall for a minute and back on to clear a temporary glitch
check the plug/socket and that the machine has power before assuming a board
washing-machine:control-panel.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): unplug before opening the console; do not probe live boards unless qualified.
washing-machine:control-panel.clarifyingQuestion: Is the display lit at all, and do some buttons work while others don't — or is the whole machine dead with no lights?
washing-machine:control-panel.secondaryQuestion: Could a child/control lock be on, and does switching off at the wall for a minute help?

washing-machine:foam-suds._approved: Story 19 — engineer-approved (Stage B). Over-sudsing. Strongly CHECK/advice-first (dose/detergent). 3-way boundary: foam dominant => foam-suds; water from drawer without foam => dispenser; genuine water leak => leak-flood. Foam escaping is a consequence, not a failed drawer/seal.
symptoms: foam coming out of the drawer
foam coming out of the door
wont spin because of the foam

components.name: detergent dose / type
supports: over-dosing
a non-HE or hand-wash detergent in an automatic/HE machine
a high-foaming detergent or mixed brands
a soft-water area (needs less)
against: the correct HE detergent at the right dose and it is still flagged (=> sensing)

components.name: re-washing already-soapy / high-suds items
supports: washing items that still hold soap
hand-washed items put through again
against: a fresh load with a correct dose

components.name: suds-lock (foam blocking drain/spin) — management
supports: foam preventing drainage or spin
the cycle extended with extra rinses
against: no drainage or spin impact

components.name: auto-dose settings / concentration [auto-dose machines ONLY]
supports: auto-dose set too high or the wrong concentration
recently refilled with concentrated detergent
against: a conventional machine with no auto-dose

components.name: false suds detection — pressure/level sensing
supports: genuine over-sudsing excluded (correct HE dose, clean system) yet a suds error persists
a pressure chamber/air-trap or sensor fault
against: obvious over-dosing or the wrong detergent (advice first)

commonConfusion.name: foam from the drawer = a failed dispenser
commonConfusion.note: Foam escaping the drawer/door is over-sudsing; the escape point is a CONSEQUENCE. Diagnose the suds (dose/detergent), not the drawer.
wouldApplyIf: WATER (not foam) is escaping, or product is left in the drawer => dispenser

commonConfusion.name: suds/foam = a leak
commonConfusion.note: Foam is not a hydraulic leak. If it's clear or dirty WATER escaping (split hose, seal, pump, tub, bearing seal) that's leak-flood.
wouldApplyIf: actual water rather than foam is escaping

commonConfusion.name: suds error = replace a part
commonConfusion.note: Almost always dosing/detergent advice; a pressure/level sensor is only suspect once genuine over-sudsing is excluded.
wouldApplyIf: the correct HE dose and a clean system, yet a persistent suds error

discriminators: 3-WAY BOUNDARY (Story-18 D-class #1 + Story-19): obvious FOAM/suds dominant => foam-suds (advice). WATER pouring from the drawer WITHOUT excessive foam => dispenser / blocked flow path. Genuine WATER leak (split hose/seal/pump/tub/bearing seal) => leak-flood. Foam escaping the drawer/door is a consequence, not a failed drawer/seal.
Strongly CHECK/advice-first: reduce dose, use the correct HE / 'for automatic machines' detergent, run rinse/drain cycles without detergent, and let suds settle before draining.
SUDS-LOCK: heavy foam can clog the pump/hoses and stop drain/spin — don't force-drain; let it settle (cross-link not-draining).
AUTO-DOSE (where fitted): check the dose setting/concentration before any pump/control part.
adviceBeforeReplacement: reduce the detergent dose and use the correct HE / automatic-machine detergent
run a rinse/drain cycle with no detergent to clear the foam; let suds settle before draining
on auto-dose machines, check the dose setting and detergent concentration
washing-machine:foam-suds.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): foam overflow makes floors slippery; do not force-drain a suds-locked pump.
washing-machine:foam-suds.clarifyingQuestion: Have you recently changed the detergent type or amount, and are you using an HE / 'for automatic machines' detergent at the right dose?
washing-machine:foam-suds.secondaryQuestion: Is it foam (not water) escaping the drawer/door, and does it keep adding rinses or refuse to spin?

washing-machine:odour._approved: Story 20 — engineer-approved (final WM completion). Smell is a CHARACTER-BASED ROUTER, not a parts node. Musty=hygiene/advice; sewage=plumbing (often not the appliance); burning=SAFETY/electrical; rubber=belt-friction; oily=bearing. Strong mechanical/electrical evidence beats generic odour.

components.name: musty/mouldy — biofilm hygiene (door seal, drawer, filter, drum)
supports: earthy musty/damp smell
visible black mould/slime in the door-seal folds, drawer or filter
frequent low-temperature or liquid-only washing
too much detergent
machine routinely left shut
smell eases with airing then returns
against: sharp sulphur smell strongest at the drain (=> plumbing)
hot/acrid burning smell (=> electrical/mechanical)

components.name: sewage/drain/sulphur — waste plumbing & installation
supports: sharp rotten-egg/sulphur smell
strongest near the standpipe/waste, or after water use
worse when unused (dry trap)
recent plumbing change / no U-bend or anti-siphon
drain hose pushed too far or no air gap
against: earthy musty that airing helps (=> hygiene)
smell only when heating/spinning (=> electrical/mechanical)

components.name: burning/electrical smell — SAFETY
supports: hot/acrid/electrical burning smell, especially on spin or heating
any smoke, melting or visible scorching
against: earthy musty (hygiene)
sulphur at the drain (plumbing)

components.name: hot rubber / friction — drive belt [belt-driven ONLY]
supports: rubbery burning smell on spin
belt-driven machine
drum stiff/slipping/restricted
against: confirmed direct-drive (no belt)
acrid electrical smell rather than rubbery

components.name: oily/greasy — bearing / drum seal
supports: oily/greasy smell with a grinding/rumble on spin
oily marks on the washing
against: no noise and no marks

commonConfusion.name: any smell = clean the machine
commonConfusion.note: Only the MUSTY/mouldy mode is a hygiene/advice issue. Drain smell is plumbing; burning is a safety/electrical stop-use; oily+noise is a bearing.
wouldApplyIf: earthy musty smell with visible mould, no burning and no drain sulphur

commonConfusion.name: smell = a failed appliance part
commonConfusion.note: Musty and sewage smells rarely need an appliance part - do not push replacements from weak hygiene/plumbing evidence.
wouldApplyIf: burning/electrical, or oily+mechanical noise, evidenced

commonConfusion.name: burning smell = just clean it
commonConfusion.note: NEVER treat a burning/electrical smell as hygiene. It is a stop-use safety situation; cross-link the electrical/mechanical cause.
wouldApplyIf: hot/acrid/electrical smell, smoke, melting or scorching

discriminators: ROUTE BY SMELL CHARACTER, do not collapse. IMPORTANT: a BURNING/acrid/electrical smell or HOT RUBBER is NOT a hygiene problem — do NOT give cleaning/maintenance advice; treat as SAFETY (stop use/unplug) and route to the electrical/mechanical fault (motor-drum/tacho/hall-sensor, tripping-electrics, or a slipping belt). OILY + grinding/rumble => drum bearing (excessive-vibration/leak-flood). MUSTY/damp/earthy => hygiene/biofilm (advice); SEWAGE/sulphur strongest at the drain => waste plumbing (often NOT the appliance).
MUSTY vs SEWAGE: musty is earthy and eases with airing then returns; sewage is sharp sulphur, intensifies near the drain and after water use (dry/again-incorrect trap).
BURNING/ELECTRICAL: active burning, smoke, melting or severe overheating => STOP USE and unplug; cross-link mains filter/wiring/motor/brushes/heater; do NOT give live-testing instructions.
ARCHITECTURE: hot-rubber/belt smell only on belt-driven machines; never suggest a belt on confirmed direct-drive.
OILY + mechanical noise/marks => bearing (excessive-vibration/leak-flood) OUTRANKS generic hygiene odour.
