washing-machine:hall-sensor._approved: Story 20 — engineer-approved (final WM completion). Direct-drive/brushless rotor-position sensing - the architecture counterpart to tacho (brushed). Never recommend carbon brushes or a conventional belt on confirmed direct-drive. 'drum not turning = hall sensor' and 'error code = hall sensor' are NOT acceptable; needs architecture + movement evidence. Rule out mechanical jam / retained water / imbalance first.

components.name: overload / imbalance / mechanical jam / retained water
supports: too many clothes or a single heavy item
drum stiff/locked or bumps/grinds when turned by hand (power OFF)
object caught between drum and tub
water still in the drum
unlevel machine
against: drum turns freely and smoothly by hand yet only twitches/won't drive under power

components.name: wiring / connector rotor-sensor to control
supports: intermittent fault or after a recent repair/move
chafed or loose loom at the sensor/motor
against: connectors sound and secure

components.name: hall / rotor-position sensor
supports: confirmed direct-drive/brushless architecture
drum free by hand but only twitches/juggles under power
cannot establish rotor position/speed
sensor open/failed where tested
against: mechanical jam/overload/retained water not excluded
a brushed machine (=> tacho/brushes)
architecture unknown

components.name: rotor / stator (magnet ring / winding)
supports: stripped rotor magnets or a failed stator winding evidenced
direct-drive, no drive with sensor & wiring good
against: cheaper causes (overload/jam/wiring/sensor) not excluded

components.name: inverter / motor-control module
supports: sensor, wiring and rotor/stator proven good
inverter/module fault indicated
against: earlier causes not excluded

commonConfusion.name: drum not turning = hall sensor
commonConfusion.note: NOT acceptable. Rule out retained water (not-draining), overload/imbalance, and a mechanical jam (hand-spin, power off) first; the hall/rotor sensor is plausible only when the drum is free by hand but movement is abnormal under power on a direct-drive machine.
wouldApplyIf: confirmed direct-drive, drum free by hand, abnormal powered twitching, water excluded

commonConfusion.name: error code = hall sensor
commonConfusion.note: Codes (e.g. LG LE/SE) are brand-specific evidence, not global mappings, and often mean overload/motor-lock as much as the sensor - interpret with make/model context.
wouldApplyIf: make/model known and its documentation maps the code to the rotor-position sensor

commonConfusion.name: carbon brushes on a direct-drive machine
commonConfusion.note: Direct-drive/brushless machines have NO carbon brushes and NO conventional belt - never recommend them; use hall/rotor-position + inverter reasoning.
wouldApplyIf: confirmed brushed/universal motor (=> tacho/brushes instead)

discriminators: ARCHITECTURE FIRST: BRUSHED => carbon brushes + commutator + conventional tacho (see tacho); BRUSHLESS/INVERTER/DIRECT-DRIVE => hall/rotor-position + stator/rotor + inverter, NO brushes, NO conventional belt. If architecture is UNKNOWN, do not confidently recommend architecture-specific parts - identify it first.

With the machine OFF, hand-rotate the drum: STIFF/locked => mechanical path (jam/bearing/foreign object); FREE + abnormal powered movement (twitch/judder, can't establish speed) => motor/sensing/control path becomes plausible.
Rule out retained water (not-draining), imbalance/overload and a jam BEFORE the sensor. Then sensor -> wiring -> rotor/stator -> inverter by evidence.
No live internal electrical testing - inspection and safe hand-rotation only.
adviceBeforeReplacement: confirm the architecture is direct-drive (motor on the back of the drum, no belt) before considering hall/rotor parts
reduce/redistribute the load and retry; with the power off, hand-spin the drum to check for a jam; power-cycle reset
check the sensor connector/loom before replacing the sensor, rotor/stator or module
washing-machine:hall-sensor.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): unplug before inspecting; no live motor/inverter testing - that is for a qualified engineer.
washing-machine:hall-sensor.clarifyingQuestion: Is it a direct-drive machine (motor bolted to the back of the drum, no belt), and with the power off does the drum turn freely by hand or is it stiff/locked?
washing-machine:hall-sensor.secondaryQuestion: Does it try to start and just twitch/judder rather than spin up, and is there an error code such as LE or SE?

washing-machine:drum-position._approved: Story 20 — engineer-approved (final WM completion). ALIGNMENT ONLY (future consolidation candidate -> hall-sensor). Not merged/deleted. Rotor/drum position sensing is the direct-drive concept covered by hall-sensor; bearing-noise phrasing belongs to the mechanical nodes.

components.name: rotor/drum position sensing (direct-drive)
supports: confirmed direct-drive/brushless architecture
abnormal powered drum movement with a free drum by hand
against: brushed machine (=> tacho)
mechanical stiffness/rumble (=> bearing)

components.name: drum bearing (if the complaint is really noise/play)
supports: deep rumble/grumble on spin, drum play/drop
against: clean electronic position/speed fault with a free drum

commonConfusion.name: drum position sensor = a distinct fault family
commonConfusion.note: On direct-drive machines this IS the hall/rotor-position sensor - see hall-sensor. Bearing noise is excessive-vibration/motor-drum. Treated as an alignment/cross-link, not a separate route.
wouldApplyIf: genuine direct-drive rotor-position evidence => hall-sensor

discriminators: Direct-drive drum/rotor position sensing => hall-sensor (rotor-position). Bearing noise/play => excessive-vibration / motor-drum. This node is an alignment/cross-link and a future consolidation candidate into hall-sensor.
ARCHITECTURE: no carbon brushes/belt on confirmed direct-drive.
washing-machine:drum-position.clarifyingQuestion: Is it a direct-drive machine, and does the drum turn freely by hand with the power off?

washing-machine:cycle-not-progressing._approved: Story 20 — engineer-approved (final WM completion). CHECK-FIRST ROUTER, not an independent parts list. Route by the STAGE it stalls on (fill/wash-heat/rinse/drain/spin/ends-early). Do NOT jump to the PCB.

components.name: STAGE = draining / water remains
supports: water left in the drum
stalls where it should empty
pump filter blocked
stuck before spin with water present
against: drains fully yet still loops (=> level sensing)

components.name: STAGE = stuck on rinse / keeps refilling — level sensing
supports: keeps filling and draining
repeated rinse / extra rinses
refills unexpectedly
blocked/kinked pressure tube (tub->switch) or faulty water-level switch
against: a single clear stall at one stage

components.name: STAGE = filling / supply
supports: stalls waiting to fill
tap part-closed or hose kinked
can't detect required flow so pauses indefinitely
against: fills normally but won't drain

components.name: STAGE = excess foam / suds-lock
supports: extra rinses added, spin inhibited, foam present
against: no foam

components.name: STAGE = washing / never heats
supports: stalls trying to reach temperature and never warms
against: stalls at fill or drain

components.name: STAGE = ends early / random stops — power/door/protection/control
supports: cuts out or ends early
power interruption
door not staying locked
overheating/protection trip
control/comms glitch (power-cycle reset helps)
against: a clear hydraulic stall at fill/drain/heat

commonConfusion.name: stuck cycle = control board
commonConfusion.note: Do NOT jump to the PCB. The commonest stalls are drainage (water remains) and level sensing (fill/drain loop). Route by stage; PCB is last.
wouldApplyIf: stage-specific hydraulic/heat/foam causes excluded and a control/comms fault is evidenced

commonConfusion.name: stuck on rinse = drain pump
commonConfusion.note: Often it can't confirm the tub is empty - check drainage AND the pressure/level sensing (tube/switch), not just the pump.
wouldApplyIf: water remains => drainage; drains fully but loops => level sensing

discriminators: ASK/DETERMINE THE STAGE FIRST: filling => inlet-valve/pressure-switch(/dispenser); washing-never-heats => heater/temperature-sensor; stuck-on-rinse/keeps-refilling => drainage -> pressure/level sensing -> inlet control -> excess foam; draining/water-remains => not-draining; before-spin => retained water/imbalance/foam/motor speed feedback; ends-early/random => power/door/overheating-protection/control-comms.
This is a ROUTER: it should not carry its own part cards - it points at the trusted stage node. Clean pump filter and check drainage FIRST (commonest stalled-cycle cause).
Do NOT jump to the main PCB without evidence.
adviceBeforeReplacement: identify exactly where it stalls (filling, washing/heating, rinsing, draining or spinning) - that points to the right node
clean the pump filter and check drainage first; check taps open and the fill hose isn't kinked; check/clear the pressure tube; reduce detergent if foaming; power-cycle for a stuck programme
washing-machine:cycle-not-progressing.clarifyingQuestion: At what point does it get stuck - filling, washing/heating, rinsing, or when it should drain or spin - and is there water left in the drum?
washing-machine:cycle-not-progressing.secondaryQuestion: Does it keep filling and draining over and over, add extra rinses, or just sit paused, or does it end early?

washing-machine:comms._approved: Story 20 — engineer-approved (final WM completion). LIGHT / ARCHITECTURE-ONLY. Only for genuine module-communication evidence. Must NOT become a broad route for dead machine (low-voltage), UI/display/button problems (control-panel), won't-start (door-lock) or motor feedback (motor-drum/tacho/hall-sensor). Main PCB is NOT the automatic first candidate.
symptoms: display not talking to the board

components.name: power-cycle / reset
supports: a transient comms glitch cleared by switching off and on
against: persists after a reset

components.name: wiring / connector between UI and main board
supports: intermittent comms error
disturbed after a repair/move
corroded/loose connector in the loom
against: connections sound and secure

components.name: user-interface / control panel board
supports: UI powered but not communicating with the main board
comms error with a good main board
against: whole machine dead (=> low-voltage)

components.name: main control PCB
supports: UI and wiring proven good and the board is not responding on the bus
against: cheaper causes (reset/wiring/UI) not excluded

commonConfusion.name: any weird behaviour = comms
commonConfusion.note: comms is only for genuine module-communication evidence. Dead machine => low-voltage; UI/display/buttons => control-panel; won't-start/door => door-lock; motor feedback => motor-drum/tacho/hall-sensor.
wouldApplyIf: a specific communication error/code with the display otherwise alive

commonConfusion.name: comms error = replace the main PCB
commonConfusion.note: Do not make the main PCB the automatic first candidate - reset and reseat/inspect the UI-to-board loom first.
wouldApplyIf: reset and wiring excluded, UI good, board unresponsive on the bus

discriminators: BOUNDARIES: completely dead => low-voltage; powered UI/display/button problem => control-panel; door prevents start => door-lock; motor speed/position feedback => motor-drum/tacho/hall-sensor; GENUINE module-communication evidence (comms code, modules not talking, display alive) => comms.
By evidence: reset -> wiring/connector -> relevant module -> main PCB. Main PCB is NOT the automatic first candidate.
Internal bus/comms is brand/architecture-specific - do not invent a universal 'communication error' meaning across brands.
adviceBeforeReplacement: power-cycle the machine to clear a transient glitch
reseat and inspect the loom/connectors between the control panel and the main board before replacing either board
washing-machine:comms.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): unplug before opening the console; no live board testing unless qualified.
washing-machine:comms.clarifyingQuestion: Is there a specific communication error code shown, and is the display otherwise lit and responding?
washing-machine:comms.secondaryQuestion: Has the machine recently been repaired or moved (a disturbed connector between the panel and the main board)?

microwave:not-heating._approved: Story 21 — engineer-approved (microwave completion). Runs-but-cold. ARCHITECTURE FIRST: conventional (transformer+magnetron+HV capacitor+HV diode) vs inverter (inverter board+magnetron). Never recommend conventional HV parts on a confirmed inverter machine or an inverter board on a confirmed conventional machine. HV safety boundary; CHECK cookware/power/door first.
symptoms: plate turns but food is cold
light and fan work but no heat
timer counts down but food stays cold

components.name: cookware / power level / mode selected
supports: non microwave-safe cookware
only the turntable/clock/light was running
a low power / defrost setting selected
against: correct microwave-safe cookware and a normal power level, still cold

components.name: door not fully latching / interlock power path
supports: door not clicking fully shut
debris on the latch
behaves as though the door is open
against: door latches firmly and it still won't heat

components.name: HV diode / rectifier [CONVENTIONAL transformer machine]
supports: conventional transformer microwave
no heat, sometimes with an abnormal heavy buzz
against: confirmed INVERTER machine (no conventional HV diode)
an ordinary DMM reading the diode open both ways does NOT prove it faulty (insufficient test voltage)

components.name: magnetron
supports: no heat with a heavy/abnormal buzz or hum
aged machine, gradual power loss
against: grill-only complaint (microwave heating works => not the magnetron)
architecture-impossible on the evidence

components.name: HV capacitor [CONVENTIONAL transformer machine]
supports: conventional machine, no heat
the internal fuse has blown
against: confirmed inverter machine
a blown fuse alone does NOT prove the capacitor

components.name: HV transformer [CONVENTIONAL transformer machine]
supports: conventional machine, no heat
against: confirmed inverter machine
if there is smoke/severe burning => STOP USE, do not keep testing

components.name: inverter board / HV module [INVERTER machine]
supports: confirmed inverter microwave, no heat
repeatable very short shutdown (~3s or ~28s) before cutting out
against: confirmed CONVENTIONAL transformer machine (do NOT recommend an inverter board)

components.name: thermal protection / cavity thermal fuse
supports: no heat after the machine got hot / cut out
thermal cutout tripped
against: never heats from cold with no thermal history

commonConfusion.name: door interlock system
commonConfusion.note: If it behaves as though the door is open (won't start / beeps), the interlock power path is the lead, not the HV parts.
wouldApplyIf: door closes but it won't start / acts like the door is open

commonConfusion.name: buzzing = magnetron only
commonConfusion.note: A heavy buzz with no heat raises BOTH the HV diode (short) and the magnetron on a conventional machine - it does not uniquely prove one component.
wouldApplyIf: conventional machine with an abnormal heavy buzz and no heat

commonConfusion.name: no heat = inverter board
commonConfusion.note: Only on a confirmed inverter machine. On a conventional machine there is no inverter board - suspect magnetron/HV diode/HV capacitor/transformer.
wouldApplyIf: confirmed inverter architecture

discriminators: ARCHITECTURE FIRST: CONVENTIONAL = transformer + magnetron + HV capacitor + HV diode; INVERTER = inverter board + magnetron. NEVER recommend an HV transformer / conventional HV capacitor / conventional HV diode on a confirmed INVERTER machine, and never recommend an inverter board on a confirmed CONVENTIONAL machine. If architecture is unknown, do not assert architecture-specific parts - identify the model first.

HEAVY/ABNORMAL BUZZ + NO HEAT on a conventional machine strongly raises an HV DIODE short OR a magnetron fault/leakage to earth - much stronger than generic 'noisy'. It does not uniquely prove one component.
SMOKE / SEVERE BURNING / transformer-area overheating => STOP USE; do not tell the customer to run it again to reproduce the fault.
INTERNAL FUSE BLOWN on a conventional machine + heating/HV behaviour raises the HV CAPACITOR / HV circuit - but the fuse is EVIDENCE, not a diagnosis; keep alternatives.
INVERTER machine + repeatable ~3-second or ~28-second shutdown before cutting out is a strong inverter/magnetron/inverter-HV fingerprint (not a universal manufacturer-independent law).

HV DIODE DMM CAVEAT: a microwave HV diode needs a much higher forward voltage than an ordinary silicon diode; many ordinary digital multimeters cannot forward-bias it on their normal diode/ohms range, so 'my normal DMM reads the new HV diode open both ways' does NOT by itself prove the replacement diode faulty (a traditional test uses an analogue meter on a high range such as Rx10K with ~9V). Do not condemn a supplied diode on that evidence.
CHECK cookware / power level / mode and that the door latches BEFORE any HV part.
adviceBeforeReplacement: confirm microwave-safe cookware, a normal power level, and that the door latches firmly
identify whether the machine is conventional or inverter (from the model) before considering architecture-specific HV parts
do not condemn a newly-supplied HV diode just because an ordinary digital multimeter reads it open in both directions - an ordinary DMM often can't provide enough test voltage
do NOT open the casing or touch/discharge/test HV components - the HV capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when unplugged
microwave:not-heating.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): a microwave HV capacitor can hold a LETHAL charge even after unplugging. Do NOT tell the customer to discharge/test/probe HV components, remove covers, bypass interlocks, or run with the door/cover compromised. Smoke/burning/violent arcing => STOP USE and unplug.
microwave:not-heating.clarifyingQuestion: Is it a conventional or an inverter microwave (check the model/rating plate), and does it make an abnormally loud/heavy buzzing when it should be heating?
microwave:not-heating.secondaryQuestion: Does it never heat at all, or does it heat then cut out after a repeatable few seconds?

safetyInformation.text: Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.
safetyInformation.hazard: High-voltage capacitor and internal circuitry can retain a dangerous charge even after the microwave is unplugged; contact can cause a severe or fatal electric shock.
safetyInformation.applicability: Any microwave internal-repair situation for this fault, independent of which internal part has failed.

microwave:low-voltage._approved: Story 21 — engineer-approved (microwave completion). Separate COMPLETELY DEAD (supply/lead/line-fuse/control) from REPEATEDLY BLOWS THE INTERNAL FUSE (downstream HV short or door monitor-switch). Fuse is EVIDENCE, not a diagnosis. HV safety boundary.

components.name: property supply / socket / plug fuse
supports: completely dead, no lights
test the socket with another appliance
house circuit tripped
against: socket proven live and the machine still dead

components.name: mains lead / internal line fuse (evidence)
supports: completely dead
internal line fuse found blown
against: display lights up (=> not a dead-power fault)

components.name: downstream HV short - HV capacitor / HV diode / magnetron [CONVENTIONAL]
supports: REPEATEDLY blows the internal fuse, especially on start/heat
conventional machine
against: simply dead with no repeated fuse blowing
confirmed inverter architecture

components.name: door monitor / interlock microswitch (a mis-timed or failed monitor switch is the classic cause of a blown line fuse)
supports: dead after the door was slammed or the fuse blew on opening/closing
monitor-switch design where a mis-timed interlock blows the fuse
against: no door-correlated failure

components.name: door catch / latch (a worn catch mis-aligns the door and mistimes the monitor switch, blowing the fuse)
supports: door feels loose, rattles, or does not latch cleanly
went dead after the catch became worn or loose
against: door latches firmly and squarely

components.name: oven lamp / bulb (a lamp that fails short commonly takes out the line fuse)
supports: went completely dead around the time the internal lamp failed
against: lamp still works or is not on the fused circuit

components.name: control / power board
supports: dead with supply proven good and the line fuse intact
against: cheaper causes (supply/lead/fuse) not excluded

commonConfusion.name: replace the fuse = fixed
commonConfusion.note: The fuse is a SYMPTOM. A fuse that blows again means a fault - find WHY it blew (downstream HV short or a monitor-switch fault). Do not just keep replacing the fuse.
wouldApplyIf: the fuse blows again after replacement

commonConfusion.name: powered but won't start = dead
commonConfusion.note: If the display works but it won't start, that is the door/interlock/control path, NOT a dead-power fault.
wouldApplyIf: display/lights work but it won't start

discriminators: COMPLETELY DEAD (no lights/display) is almost always a blown internal line fuse - but the fuse is EVIDENCE, not the diagnosis: find what blew it. List the likely causes to check: the property supply / plug fuse, the mains lead, the door monitor / interlock microswitch (the classic culprit), a worn door catch that mistimes that switch, the oven lamp / bulb (a shorted lamp takes out the fuse), and on a conventional machine a downstream HV short (HV capacitor / HV diode / magnetron); the control board only once the cheaper causes are excluded.
REPEATEDLY BLOWS THE INTERNAL FUSE => the same downstream causes (door monitor-switch, HV capacitor / HV diode / magnetron on a conventional machine) - the fuse is EVIDENCE, not the diagnosis.
Do NOT encode 'replace fuse = fixed' - a repeatedly blowing fuse means an upstream/downstream fault to find.
POWERED but WON'T START (display alive) is NOT this node => door/interlock/control.
adviceBeforeReplacement: check the wall socket with another appliance and the plug fuse where fitted
if the internal fuse blows again, the cause is elsewhere - do not keep replacing it
do NOT open the casing or touch HV components - stored charge is lethal
microwave:low-voltage.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): a microwave HV capacitor can hold a LETHAL charge even after unplugging. Do NOT tell the customer to discharge/test/probe HV components, remove covers, bypass interlocks, or run with the door/cover compromised. Smoke/burning/violent arcing => STOP USE and unplug.
microwave:low-voltage.clarifyingQuestion: Is the microwave completely dead with no lights or display, or does it power up but blow the fuse (or refuse to start)?
microwave:low-voltage.secondaryQuestion: If it blows the fuse, does it do so as soon as you switch on, or only when it starts to heat?

microwave:sparking-arcing._approved: Story 21 — engineer-approved (microwave completion). Determine WHERE the arcing is and WHAT was in the cavity. CHECK metal/foil/contamination first; waveguide (mica) cover is the top non-metal cause; magnetron last. STOP USE on violent/repeated arcing or burning/cavity damage.
symptoms: the little cardboard bit is sparking
paper bit on the side is sparking
little plate on the side wall sparking
burnt square on the side wall
that thing on the side wall is arcing

components.name: metal / foil / metallic-trim in the cavity
supports: a metal object, foil, twist-tie or dish with metallic decoration/rim was inside
arcing only with certain items
against: nothing metallic present and it still arcs

components.name: food / grease contamination on the waveguide cover
supports: dirty/greasy cavity
arcing at the mica cover with food splatter
against: clean cavity and cover

components.name: contamination / damage at the door edge or perimeter (door face / choke / front frame)
supports: the arcing is at the DOOR EDGE / around the door frame, not a spot on the side/roof panel
food/carbon debris or burn marks on the door face, the front cavity frame, or the choke area
arcing appeared after spills built up around the door mouth
against: the arcing is at a spot on the side/roof panel (the mica / waveguide cover)
a metal object or foil is in the cavity
the door face, frame and choke are clean and undamaged

components.name: waveguide (mica) cover damaged
supports: burnt / blackened / holed mica cover
carbon tracking on the cover
repeated arcing at the cover on the side/roof
against: cover clean and intact

components.name: cavity paint / coating damage
supports: chipped paint exposing bare metal, or rust in the cavity
against: intact cavity coating

components.name: magnetron / cavity (last)
supports: arcing persists with a clean cavity, an intact cover and no metal present
against: metal in the cavity, a dirty or damaged waveguide cover, or chipped paint not yet addressed

commonConfusion.name: arcing = magnetron
commonConfusion.note: Usually metal in the cavity or a burnt/dirty waveguide (mica) cover. Do NOT jump to the magnetron - it is the last suspect after the cavity/cover are cleared.
wouldApplyIf: clean cavity, intact cover, no metal, yet still arcing

commonConfusion.name: cavity arcing = door seal / gasket
commonConfusion.note: A domestic microwave has NO user-serviceable door seal/gasket. Arcing INSIDE the cavity (side/roof panel or floor) is the waveguide (mica) cover, food/metal contamination, or a metal object - never lead with a 'door seal'. Only arcing located specifically at the DOOR EDGE raises the door face/choke/front-frame (contamination or damage), not a replaceable seal.
wouldApplyIf: the arcing is inside the cavity (side/roof panel or floor) rather than specifically at the door edge

discriminators: FIRST determine WHERE the sparking is and WHAT was in the cavity. A metal object / foil / metallic-trimmed dish anywhere => remove it FIRST (user cause); this LEADS whenever the customer says something metallic was inside. Arcing at the mica/waveguide cover with burning or carbon marks => the waveguide cover (clean or replace). Chipped paint / bare metal => cavity coating. Only a clean cavity + intact cover + no metal raises the magnetron.

LOCATION is the highest-value discriminator: arcing at a SPOT ON THE SIDE/ROOF PANEL => the waveguide (mica) cover; arcing at the CAVITY FLOOR/WALL => contamination / coating damage / exposed metal / a foreign object; arcing at the DOOR EDGE / around the door frame => contamination or damage at the door face/choke/front frame (clean food/carbon debris there; a genuinely damaged door needs professional attention). If the LOCATION is unknown, advise a safe visual inspection (unplugged) before naming a part.

DO NOT lead with a 'door seal / gasket' for arcing INSIDE the cavity: a domestic microwave has no user-serviceable door seal, and cavity arcing (side/roof/floor) points to the waveguide cover / contamination / metal - only DOOR-EDGE-located arcing raises the door face/choke/perimeter.
STOP USE if the arcing is violent/repeated, or there is burning or visible cavity/cover damage - do not keep running it to 'see if it clears'.
adviceBeforeReplacement: note WHERE the sparking is (a spot on the side/roof panel, the cavity floor, or the door edge) and whether anything metallic was inside - this is what decides the cause
remove any metal/foil and any dish with metallic trim; use only microwave-safe cookware
visually inspect the waveguide (mica) cover for burning/carbon and gently clean food/grease off it
if the sparking is at the door edge, gently clean food/carbon debris from the door face and front frame
stop using it if the arcing is violent/repeated or there is burning or cavity damage
do not run the microwave with a damaged waveguide cover or cavity
microwave:sparking-arcing.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): violent/repeated arcing, burning, or visible cavity/waveguide-cover damage => STOP USE and unplug. Do not operate with a damaged cover/cavity or removed covers; do not touch HV components (stored charge).
microwave:sparking-arcing.clarifyingQuestion: Where is the sparking coming from - a metal object/dish in the cavity, or a spot on the side/roof panel (the mica cover) - and was anything metallic inside?
microwave:sparking-arcing.secondaryQuestion: Is the mica cover on the side/roof burnt, blackened or holed?

microwave:main-pcb._approved: Story 21 — engineer-approved (microwave completion). Controls/keypad/display. Down-rank the main PCB: keypad/membrane and display module are the common causes; completely dead => low-voltage; door prevents start => door. Adds keypad vocabulary.
symptoms: display dead but it still works

components.name: control lock / demo mode
supports: all buttons locked out
a lock/child-lock symbol shown
a reset/power-cycle restores it
against: only certain buttons dead while others work

components.name: keypad / membrane / touchpad
supports: some buttons work and others don't
specific digits/functions unresponsive
sticky or damaged membrane, display otherwise fine
against: the whole panel and display are dead (=> supply)

components.name: control panel / fascia
supports: fascia/selector physically damaged
a rotary/selector control fault
against: a flat membrane keypad issue with a good fascia

components.name: display / UI module
supports: display blank/partial/garbled but the machine otherwise runs
against: a keypad-only issue with a good display

components.name: main control PCB
supports: keypad, fascia and display proven good and it still won't respond
against: cheaper causes (lock/keypad/display) not excluded

commonConfusion.name: controls = main PCB
commonConfusion.note: Down-rank the PCB. A dead/partial keypad is usually the membrane; a blank/garbled display is usually the display module. The main PCB is the last suspect.
wouldApplyIf: keypad, membrane and display module proven good

commonConfusion.name: unresponsive = broken
commonConfusion.note: Completely dead (no lights) => low-voltage/supply; door-prevents-start/beeps => door. Not every control problem is the control board.
wouldApplyIf: completely dead => low-voltage; beeps/won't start => door

discriminators: KEYPAD-ONLY (some buttons dead, display fine) => keypad/membrane. DISPLAY-ONLY (blank/garbled but the machine runs) => display/UI module. Check a control/child lock first. COMPLETELY DEAD => low-voltage. DOOR prevents start / beeps => door. Main PCB is the LAST suspect.
A stuck single button or specific unresponsive digits point to the membrane, not the whole board.
adviceBeforeReplacement: check for a control/child lock and try a power-cycle reset
note whether it's some buttons (membrane) or the display (module) or completely dead (supply)
microwave:main-pcb.safety: ADVISORY ONLY: unplug before inspecting the console; HV stored charge - do not open beyond the accessible fascia.
microwave:main-pcb.clarifyingQuestion: Is the display still lit and working while only some buttons fail, or is the display itself blank/garbled - or is the whole machine dead?
microwave:main-pcb.secondaryQuestion: Do some buttons still work, and does a power-cycle at the wall change anything?

microwave:cutting-out._approved: Story 21 — engineer-approved (microwave completion). Split by TIMING: repeatable very-short shutdown (~3s/~28s, esp inverter) vs runs-minutes-then-hot (cooling/thermal) vs random loss (supply/door/control). Don't collapse into one cause.
symptoms: cuts out after a few seconds

components.name: inverter / magnetron / HV feedback [repeatable seconds shutdown]
supports: confirmed INVERTER machine
repeatable very short shutdown (~3s or ~28s) before cutting out
no heat during the short run
against: runs for minutes then stops when hot (=> cooling/thermal)
conventional machine

components.name: cooling fan / blocked airflow / vents
supports: runs several minutes then stops when hot
dusty/blocked vents or against a wall
against: cuts out within seconds

components.name: thermal cutout / protection
supports: cuts out when hot and resets after cooling
repeated overheating trips
against: cuts out cold within seconds

components.name: overheating magnetron / HV system
supports: repeated thermal cutout with airflow proven clear
against: a simple blocked vent / dusty fan explains it

components.name: supply / door-interlock / control [random loss]
supports: random power loss
intermittent when the door is nudged
loose plug / marginal socket
against: a consistent thermal or fixed-seconds pattern

commonConfusion.name: cuts out = overheating
commonConfusion.note: Only if it runs for MINUTES and gets hot. A repeatable few-seconds cut-out (esp inverter) is the inverter/magnetron/HV feedback path; random loss is supply/door/control.
wouldApplyIf: runs minutes then stops when hot

discriminators: A) REPEATABLE VERY SHORT shutdown (~3s / ~28s), especially a confirmed inverter machine => inverter / magnetron / HV feedback path (see not-heating); strong fingerprint, not a universal law. B) RUNS FOR MINUTES then stops / gets hot => cooling fan / blocked airflow / thermal cutout / overheating magnetron. C) RANDOM power loss => supply / door-interlock / thermal / control. Do not collapse all cutting-out into one cause.
Fixed-seconds timing without confirmed architecture should not become certainty.
adviceBeforeReplacement: note the timing (a few seconds vs several minutes vs random) and whether it gets hot
check the vents aren't blocked and the machine has airflow
identify conventional vs inverter for the seconds-shutdown pattern
microwave:cutting-out.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): a microwave HV capacitor can hold a LETHAL charge even after unplugging. Do NOT tell the customer to discharge/test/probe HV components, remove covers, bypass interlocks, or run with the door/cover compromised. Smoke/burning/violent arcing => STOP USE and unplug.
microwave:cutting-out.clarifyingQuestion: Does it cut out after a repeatable few seconds, after several minutes once it's hot, or at random?
microwave:cutting-out.secondaryQuestion: Is it a conventional or inverter microwave, and does it get hot before it stops?

microwave:noisy._approved: Story 21 — engineer-approved (microwave completion). Route by sound CHARACTER + location. Do not use 'noisy = magnetron': only a heavy electrical buzz WITH no heat raises the HV/magnetron path.

components.name: turntable drive - roller ring / coupler / motor / obstruction
supports: grinding/clicking from the BASE as the plate turns
tray dragging or an obstruction
worn roller wheels
against: noise with the turntable removed
a heavy electrical buzz

components.name: cooling fan / fan obstruction / fan motor
supports: whirring/airflow noise
rattle from the fan area
noise rises with running time
against: grinding tied to the plate turning

components.name: HV / magnetron path [heavy buzz + NO HEAT]
supports: a heavy electrical BUZZ together with NO HEATING
conventional machine buzzing loudly
against: it still heats normally (=> mechanical noise, not HV)

components.name: loose tray / rack / support / panel
supports: mechanical rattle from a loose part or the rack/support
against: a deep electrical buzz or base grinding

commonConfusion.name: noisy = magnetron
commonConfusion.note: Only a HEAVY electrical buzz WITH no heat raises the HV/magnetron path. Grinding from the base = turntable drive; whirring = fan; rattle = a loose part.
wouldApplyIf: a heavy buzz together with no heating

discriminators: Route by CHARACTER + location: GRINDING/CLICKING from the base as the plate turns => turntable roller ring / coupler / motor / obstruction; WHIRRING / airflow => cooling fan / obstruction / fan motor; HEAVY electrical BUZZ + NO HEAT => HV/magnetron path (architecture-dependent, see not-heating); CRACKLING => arcing (see sparking-arcing); RATTLE => a loose tray/rack/support or the fan. Do not use 'microwave noisy => magnetron'.
adviceBeforeReplacement: note the sound character and where it comes from; try running with the turntable removed to isolate base-drive noise
if it's a heavy buzz, check whether it still heats
microwave:noisy.safety: ADVISORY ONLY: a heavy buzz with burning/no heat - stop use; HV stored charge, do not open.
microwave:noisy.clarifyingQuestion: What does the noise sound like and where does it come from - grinding from the base, a whirring fan, a heavy electrical buzz, or a rattle?
microwave:noisy.secondaryQuestion: Does it still heat the food normally while it's noisy?

microwave:lighting._approved: Story 21 — engineer-approved (microwave completion). Proportionate: if only the cavity lamp fails and everything else is normal => lamp then holder/wiring. Don't overdiagnose; broader electrical symptoms route elsewhere.

components.name: cavity lamp / bulb
supports: only the light has failed and the microwave otherwise works normally
against: broader electrical symptoms (won't heat / dead / display issues)

components.name: lamp holder / wiring
supports: a known-good lamp still doesn't light
against: the machine has other electrical faults

commonConfusion.name: no light = board fault
commonConfusion.note: If ONLY the lamp is out and everything else works, it's the lamp/holder - not the PCB. Broader symptoms route to low-voltage/main-pcb.
wouldApplyIf: other electrical symptoms present alongside the light failure

discriminators: If ONLY the cavity lamp has failed and everything else is normal => lamp, then holder/wiring. If there are broader electrical symptoms, route accordingly (low-voltage / main-pcb). Do not overdiagnose a simple lamp.
adviceBeforeReplacement: confirm the rest of the microwave works normally before assuming anything beyond the lamp
microwave:lighting.safety: ADVISORY ONLY: unplug before changing a lamp; HV stored charge - do not go beyond the accessible lamp access.
microwave:lighting.clarifyingQuestion: Does the microwave otherwise work normally (heats, turns, display) and only the inside light has failed?

microwave:grill-not-heating._approved: Story 21 — engineer-approved (microwave completion). Grill/combi element not heating while MICROWAVE heating works - strong AGAINST the magnetron/HV. Only on models with a grill.

components.name: grill/combi mode selected correctly
supports: unsure whether grill/combi mode was actually selected
against: grill mode confirmed selected and still cold

components.name: grill element
supports: microwave heating works but the grill doesn't glow/get hot
the element looks broken/blistered/open
against: NEITHER microwave nor grill heats (=> shared supply/control, not the element)

components.name: grill thermal cutout / thermal fuse
supports: grill worked then stopped
signs of overheating
against: grill never worked from new

components.name: grill relay / control
supports: the element is proven good but never gets switched on
against: the element itself hasn't been checked

components.name: wiring to the grill element
supports: intermittent grill heating
a disturbed/loose connection to the element
against: solid connections

commonConfusion.name: grill won't heat = magnetron / HV
commonConfusion.note: If the MICROWAVE function heats normally, the magnetron/HV generation is working - the grill fault is the grill element, its thermal protection, the relay/control or wiring. If NEITHER microwave nor grill heats, that's a shared supply/control problem (see not-heating / low-voltage).
wouldApplyIf: microwave heating works but the grill doesn't

discriminators: GRILL-ONLY not heating while the MICROWAVE function heats fine is STRONG AGAINST the magnetron / microwave HV generation - suspect the grill element, its thermal protection, the relay/control, or wiring.
If NEITHER microwave nor grill heats, that's a shared supply/control problem (see not-heating / low-voltage), not the grill element.
Grill/combi only exists on models with a grill.
adviceBeforeReplacement: confirm the microwave function itself still heats (that clears the magnetron/HV)
confirm grill/combi mode was actually selected
do NOT open the casing or touch HV components - stored charge is lethal
microwave:grill-not-heating.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety authoritative): grill elements get very hot; unplug before inspection; HV stored charge - do not open beyond the cavity.
microwave:grill-not-heating.clarifyingQuestion: Does the normal microwave function still heat food, and it's only the grill that won't get hot?
microwave:grill-not-heating.secondaryQuestion: Did the grill work before and then stop, or has it never worked?

oven-cooker:terminal-block._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). Mains terminal block where the fixed supply cable enters the oven is a common real-world failure - the connection overheats/burns. Completely dead / intermittent / burning smell / melted connector. STOP USE; no live/fixed-wiring instructions.
symptoms: burning smell from the back of the oven
burnt smell where the cable comes in

components.name: external supply / isolator / house circuit
supports: completely dead - check the cooker switch/isolator and the house circuit first
against: supply proven live and a burnt smell/heat damage at the oven

components.name: mains terminal block / incoming connection
supports: burning smell / burnt or melted connector where the mains cable enters
discoloured/charred terminal, white powdery residue
intermittent power or power lost under load
completely dead with heat damage at the connection
against: no heat damage and the fault is a cold no-heat in one mode (=> element)

components.name: incoming cable / fixed wiring
supports: heat damage extends onto the supply cable
loose fixed-wiring connection
against: damage confined to the block/oven side

components.name: heating element causing terminal overheat
supports: an element shorting to its sheath can overheat/burn the terminal it connects to
against: burn is clearly at the incoming mains block, not an element tag

commonConfusion.name: burnt connection = PCB
commonConfusion.note: A burnt terminal block / incoming connection is a supply-connection failure, not the control board. Address the connection (and any element that caused it), not the PCB.
wouldApplyIf: heat damage/burning is at the mains connection or element tags

discriminators: The mains TERMINAL BLOCK where the fixed supply cable enters the oven commonly overheats and burns (high-resistance/loose connection, undersized, or an element shorting to its sheath). Signs: burning smell from the back, charred/melted/discoloured connector, white powdery residue, intermittent power or power lost under load, or completely dead with heat damage.
STRONG VISIBLE BURNING/MELTING => STOP USE and isolate the supply; do NOT keep operating it.
A failing element can burn its terminal - check the element as well as the block.
Completely dead with NO heat damage/burning => check the external supply/isolator first, then the block, wiring and control - do not assume the block without evidence.
adviceBeforeReplacement: if there is a burning smell or visible melting/charring at the connection, STOP USE and isolate the supply at the cooker switch/consumer unit
this is a fixed-mains connection - it should be inspected/repaired by a qualified person, not worked on live
oven-cooker:terminal-block.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:terminal-block.clarifyingQuestion: Is there a burning smell or visible melting/charring at the back where the mains cable connects, and is the oven completely dead or intermittent?
oven-cooker:terminal-block.secondaryQuestion: Has the power been lost suddenly or does it come and go under load?

oven-cooker:cooling-fan._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). Cooling fan (cools controls/cabinet) is DIFFERENT from the cavity/cooking fan. Failure => electronics overheat => thermal cutout => oven cuts out when hot, recovers when cool. Failed cooling fan is a SAFETY issue - stop use.
symptoms: oven cuts out when it gets hot then works again when cool
kitchen units above the oven getting warm
oven shuts off after a while when hot

components.name: airflow / vents obstruction
supports: vents blocked / oven boxed in with poor airflow
against: airflow clear and the cooling fan still not running

components.name: cooling fan motor
supports: the quiet whirring cooling fan isn't running
controls/fascia/cabinetry getting hot
oven overheats and cuts out then recovers when cool
against: it's the cavity fan (uneven cooking / fan-only mode) not turning (=> fan motor)

components.name: cooling-fan thermostat / control
supports: cooling fan never starts even when hot
fan control/switch not energising the fan
against: fan motor itself proven seized/open

components.name: overheat thermal cut-out
supports: oven cuts out on overheat because cooling failed; may not reset
against: no overheating - a straight no-heat or trip

commonConfusion.name: cuts out when hot = thermostat
commonConfusion.note: If it cuts out when hot and RECOVERS when cool, suspect the COOLING fan / airflow / thermal cutout, not just the thermostat. If it TRIPS THE RCD, that's element earth leakage instead.
wouldApplyIf: cuts out hot and recovers when cool, no RCD trip

commonConfusion.name: cooling fan = cooking fan
commonConfusion.note: The cooling fan cools the controls/cabinet (quiet whirring, top/rear); the cavity/cooking fan circulates heat around the food. Different components and symptoms.
wouldApplyIf: uneven cooking / fan-only mode not turning => cavity fan (fan-motor)

discriminators: The COOLING fan (cools the controls/cabinet - a quiet whirring during/after cooking) is a DIFFERENT component from the CAVITY/COOKING fan (circulates heat around the food). Uneven cooking / fan-only-mode not turning => cavity fan (fan-motor); controls/fascia getting hot or cuts-out-when-hot-recovers-when-cool => cooling fan.

CAUSAL CHAIN: cooling fan fails => controls/electronics overheat => overheat thermal cutout operates => oven cuts out; often works again after cooling. Consider cooling fan / its thermostat / airflow / thermal cutout.
SAFETY: a failed cooling fan lets the controls, fascia and surrounding units overheat (distortion/fire risk) - advise stopping use until repaired.
adviceBeforeReplacement: work out which fan: cavity fan (uneven cooking) vs cooling fan (quiet whirring, controls getting hot)
if the controls/fascia are getting hot, stop using the oven until the cooling fan is repaired
oven-cooker:cooling-fan.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply. A failed cooling fan is a safety issue - stop use until repaired.
oven-cooker:cooling-fan.clarifyingQuestion: Does it cut out only once it's hot and work again after cooling, and are the controls or the fascia getting hot?
oven-cooker:cooling-fan.secondaryQuestion: Is it the quiet cooling fan (controls area) that's stopped, or the cavity fan that circulates heat around the food?

oven-cooker:temperature-probe._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). Electronic oven temperature sensor (NTC/PT). Architecture counterpart to the mechanical thermostat. Temperature-incorrect / sensor error on electronic ovens.

components.name: oven temperature sensor (NTC/PT) [electronic ovens]
supports: electronic-control oven with wrong/erratic temperature or a sensor error
open/short sensor reading
against: a mechanical dial-thermostat oven (=> thermostat)

components.name: sensor wiring / connector
supports: intermittent temperature error, disturbed connector
against: solid wiring

components.name: control board (last)
supports: sensor and wiring proven good, control misreads
against: cheaper causes unchecked

commonConfusion.name: temperature wrong = thermostat
commonConfusion.note: On an ELECTRONIC oven the regulating device is the temperature sensor + control, not a mechanical thermostat. Identify the control type.
wouldApplyIf: electronic oven with a digital temperature display

discriminators: ELECTRONIC ovens regulate via a temperature SENSOR (NTC/PT) + control board; MECHANICAL ovens use a dial thermostat + capillary. Route temperature-incorrect to the sensor on electronic ovens, to the thermostat on mechanical ones. Sensor before board.
Manufacturer sensor error codes are supporting evidence with make/model context, not universal mappings.
adviceBeforeReplacement: identify whether the oven is electronic (digital) or a mechanical dial thermostat
check the sensor connector before the control board
oven-cooker:temperature-probe.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:temperature-probe.clarifyingQuestion: Is it an electronic oven with a digital temperature display, and is the temperature wrong or is there a sensor error shown?

oven-cooker:selector-switch._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). Function selector: when only particular functions/positions work. A selector can fail on individual contacts - don't always blame the element of the failed function. Also check clock-AUTO where relevant.

components.name: clock/timer AUTO (if the whole oven won't run)
supports: oven won't run at all after a power cut - set MANUAL first
against: specific functions fail while others work

components.name: main function / selector switch
supports: several loads fail only on particular selector positions
a component works via a different position that uses it
only certain positions work / intermittent with position
knob spins freely / doesn't engage
a function stuck on / won't switch off
against: a single element open with the selector switching other modes correctly

components.name: grill energy regulator / simmerstat
supports: grill-mode heat/glow incomplete while top-oven cooking on the same system is normal
grill control does not vary grill power as expected
against: every function dead
a visibly failed element with no mode-specific split

components.name: control PCB (last)
supports: selector proven good and functions still misbehave
against: classic selector-contact pattern not excluded

commonConfusion.name: function dead = that element is bad
commonConfusion.note: Not always, and not automatically the selector either. A selector can fail on individual contacts. If the SAME heating system behaves differently by mode (top-oven vs grill), keep the mode-specific control/supply path AND the element in play. Do not conclude 'works in another mode therefore selector' or 'grill partly heats therefore element'.
wouldApplyIf: the same element works via another position, or multiple loads fail on one selector position

discriminators: When only PARTICULAR functions/positions work, the MAIN SELECTOR/FUNCTION SWITCH is a candidate — it commonly performs the switching between top-oven (element sections in series, ~half mains) and grill (full mains). That is not a deterministic selector diagnosis.

Cross-mode evidence is valuable: heats in top-oven but grill glow/toast is incomplete => reason about the mode-specific control/supply path (selector, grill energy regulator/simmerstat, wiring) as well as the element. Do not conclude 'element works in another mode therefore selector' or 'grill partly heats therefore element'.
If the WHOLE oven will not run (especially after a power cut), the flashing-programmer / AUTO use-condition comes first — advice, not a selector.

A visibly open single element (other modes switching correctly) keeps the element in play; burnt selector contacts/terminals remain legitimate when evidence warrants them. Do not always recommend the selector.
adviceBeforeReplacement: check whether the same element works via another compatible mode/position
after a power cut, set the clock to MANUAL first
oven-cooker:selector-switch.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:selector-switch.clarifyingQuestion: Which functions/positions work and which don't - and does any affected element work via a different mode?
oven-cooker:selector-switch.secondaryQuestion: Does the selector knob engage properly or spin freely?

mediaInformation.title: About uneven oven heating
mediaInformation.description: When an oven cooks unevenly or browns on one side, the parts usually involved are the fan that circulates the heat, the element, the temperature sensor and the door seal. This reference shows where they sit and the safe checks worth making. Replacing these parts is a job for a qualified engineer.
mediaInformation.relatedCheck: identify the parts behind uneven oven heating and the safe pre-checks
mediaInformation.alt: Reference diagram: an oven showing the parts involved in even heating — fan, element, temperature sensor and door seal — with customer-safe checks

provenance.title: WhichPart generic appliance reference diagram
provenance.basis: Identifies the parts behind uneven oven heating for a grounded oven-cooker:uneven-heating diagnosis. ABOUT identification/explanation only — not a DIY repair instruction.

oven-cooker:uneven-heating._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). CHECK-first: circulation (cavity fan), door seal/alignment, tray/loading before selling a thermostat. One-side-consistently affected raises fan circulation.

components.name: loading / tray position / airflow
supports: overloaded, trays blocking airflow, food too close to one element
against: consistent one-sided pattern regardless of loading

components.name: cavity fan motor / blade (poor hot-air circulation is the usual cause of uneven fan-oven cooking)
supports: one side consistently under/over-cooked
fan slow, noisy, or blade distorted (poor circulation)
against: conventional (non-fan) mode only

components.name: door seal / door alignment (heat escaping one side)
supports: heat escaping one side, visible seal damage or a door that doesn't sit flush
against: seal and door sound

components.name: a missing element in the selected mode
supports: one of the elements for that mode has failed so heat comes from one side
against: all elements for the mode working

components.name: thermostat/sensor (last for uneven)
supports: temperature control clearly off as well
against: temperature is about right overall, just uneven

commonConfusion.name: uneven = thermostat
commonConfusion.note: Uneven cooking is usually circulation (cavity fan/blade), door seal/alignment or loading - check those before selling a thermostat.
wouldApplyIf: temperature control is otherwise fine, just uneven

discriminators: Uneven/one-sided cooking is CHECK-first: loading/tray/airflow, then cavity FAN circulation (slow fan / distorted blade), then DOOR SEAL / alignment (heat escaping), then a missing element for that mode. Thermostat/sensor last.
One side CONSISTENTLY hotter/cooler regardless of loading points to circulation or a door-seal/alignment gap.
adviceBeforeReplacement: check loading/tray position and that the cavity fan spins
inspect the door seal and that the door closes flush
oven-cooker:uneven-heating.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:uneven-heating.clarifyingQuestion: Is it always the same side, and is the fan spinning and the door sealing/closing properly?

oven-cooker:door-seal._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). Usually visually obvious. Contributes to slow/uneven heating and heat escape. Ground on clear visible damage.
symptoms: rubber seal on the door damaged

components.name: oven door seal / gasket
supports: visible split/perished/loose/missing-section seal
heat escaping around the door
slow or uneven heating with a damaged seal
against: seal intact and seated (look elsewhere for slow/uneven heat)

commonConfusion.name: slow heating = element
commonConfusion.note: A damaged/hanging door seal lets heat escape and can cause slow/uneven heating - check the visible seal before an element/thermostat.
wouldApplyIf: visible seal damage or a gap with heat escaping

discriminators: Oven door-seal failure is usually VISUALLY OBVIOUS (split, hanging loose, missing a section, hardened, obvious gap). If clearly visible, ground the seal. It can contribute to slow heating, poor temperature performance, uneven cooking and heat escaping - but confirm it's visibly damaged.
adviceBeforeReplacement: visually check the seal all round for splits/gaps/missing sections
oven-cooker:door-seal.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): built-in ovens run on mains and are often hard-wired. Do NOT instruct the customer to work on live/fixed mains wiring, open a live terminal block, perform live-voltage or insulation-resistance tests, bypass thermal protection or the RCD, or repeatedly reset/energise a burning or tripping oven. Burning/melting/smoke or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate the supply.
oven-cooker:door-seal.clarifyingQuestion: Is the door seal visibly split, hanging loose or missing a section, and is heat escaping around the door?

oven-cooker:door-hinge._approved: Story 22 — engineer-approved (built-in electric oven completion). Usually visually/mechanically obvious. Poor closure can cause apparent heating/cooking problems.

components.name: door hinge
supports: door drops/sags, won't stay shut, springs open, feels loose
a visibly bent/broken hinge
against: hinges sound and the door closes flush (=> seal/alignment)

components.name: hinge receiver / support [where fitted]
supports: the hinge slot/receiver in the cabinet is damaged
against: receiver sound

components.name: door alignment / structure

against: the door physically won't latch (=> latch/alignment)

components.name: main control board / PCB (last)
supports: the loom, connectors and the driven components are all proven good and the wiring is intact
against: the fault changes with door movement or is several unrelated intermittent errors (=> loom first)

commonConfusion.name: multiple errors = several failed parts
commonConfusion.note: Several unrelated, intermittent errors (a heating error, then a door error, then the dispenser) that come and go are far more likely ONE common wiring/door-loom fault than several parts failing at once. Do not sell heater + latch + dispenser + PCB independently.

commonConfusion.name: intermittent fault = PCB
commonConfusion.note: The dishwasher's controls and their wiring run through the door and flex every time it opens; intermittent or door-position faults point to the loom before the PCB.

commonConfusion.name: component not powered = component faulty
commonConfusion.note: A part that tests good but never receives power is usually a broken drive wire - often in the door loom - not the part itself.
wouldApplyIf: the part appears good but gets no drive

discriminators: The dishwasher has a large moving door; the wiring for the door-mounted controls, door switch, dispenser and often the heater/sensor sense runs down through the hinge/flex area and flexes on every open and close. Over years individual conductors fatigue, chafe, pinch or break, giving INTERMITTENT and apparently UNRELATED faults.

STRONGLY raise the door loom when: (a) several unrelated errors come and go, (b) the fault changes when the door is opened/closed/moved or the machine starts if the door is jiggled, or (c) a component tests good but is never being driven. In all three, suspect the LOOM BEFORE condemning the PCB or replacing several parts.

The point of the reasoning is not to name the exact broken conductor: repeated door flex -> a broken/chafed wire -> an apparently unrelated component or control symptom. A qualified engineer confirms with the power off.
Do NOT ask the customer to test or manipulate the loom while the machine is powered.

commonConfusion.name: weak spray = circulation pump
commonConfusion.note: If the machine is UNDERFILLED (only a little water goes in), weak spray is a FILL / water-delivery problem, not the circulation pump. Diagnose the pump only when the tub fills to the correct level but spray is still weak.
wouldApplyIf: the tub is clearly underfilled

commonConfusion.name: every dishwasher has a matrix
commonConfusion.note: The side water matrix / heat exchanger is architecture-specific (common on Bosch-group machines). Do not recommend matrix/heat-exchanger parts on a machine that doesn't have one - identify the model first.
wouldApplyIf: the architecture is unknown or the machine has no side water system

commonConfusion.name: [S24] weak spray = circulation pump (scaled matrix)
commonConfusion.note: On a confirmed side-matrix machine, heavy scale/deposits in the matrix waterways can restrict water delivery -> underfill -> weak spray. That is a restricted water path, not the circulation pump. Confirm the fill level first.
wouldApplyIf: a confirmed side-matrix machine with visible scaling and underfill

discriminators: Some dishwashers (notably Bosch-group) use a tall side WATER MATRIX / LABYRINTH / HEAT EXCHANGER that stores and routes water and aids condensation drying and softening/regeneration. On those machines treat supply -> inlet valve -> inlet filter -> matrix/exchanger -> valves -> flow/level sensing -> tub fill as one connected water-delivery system.

UNDERFILL vs CIRCULATION: fills with only a small amount of water + weak spray => a FILL / matrix / flow-level problem, NOT automatically the circulation pump. A restricted matrix, partial inlet valve or flow/level fault starves the arms. Only suspect the circulation pump when the tub fills to the correct level but spray is still weak.

Matrix/exchanger faults are architecture-specific - confirm the machine actually has one (model/appearance) before recommending matrix parts. Error-code meaning stays manufacturer/model-specific (e.g. some Bosch codes relate to the heat exchanger only on relevant machines); do not universalise codes.

[S24] Hard water is EVIDENCE, not proof: a hard-water area PLUS progressive water-path symptoms PLUS visible scale/restriction raises a scale/restriction cause - hard-water location ALONE is never a diagnosis.

[S24] Narrow matrix/labyrinth waterways progressively accumulate scale/deposits in hard-water areas -> reduced/incorrect water delivery -> underfill -> weak spray -> poor wash (or abnormal fill/level behaviour). Visible heavy scaling in the side matrix + low water + weak spray strongly favours a restricted matrix/water-delivery path OVER the circulation pump. Architecture-first still applies: a machine with no side matrix cannot have a scaled one.

[S24] PROGRESSIVE vs SUDDEN: gradual worsening favours scale/restriction/contamination; a sudden failure (worked yesterday, dead/completely different today) favours a discrete blockage, failed component, electrical fault or leak - not scale. Not absolute.
adviceBeforeReplacement: identify the make/model and whether it has a side water system
confirm whether the tub actually underfills or fills normally
check the supply, tap and inlet filter first

commonConfusion.note: A split or misdirected spray arm can fire water sideways at the door and look like a failed seal. If the leak is only during washing and the lower arm is split/cracked, the ARM is the cause - check it before selling a seal.
wouldApplyIf: a leak at the door only while washing plus a damaged arm

commonConfusion.name: both arms weak = both arms failed
commonConfusion.note: If BOTH arms are weak it's almost never two failed arms - look for a common upstream cause: underfill/low water or weak circulation.
wouldApplyIf: all spray action is weak

commonConfusion.name: arm not spinning = circulation pump
commonConfusion.note: An arm that won't spin is most often blocked (jets/debris) or catching on dishes - clear it first; suspect the pump only once the arm is clear and water flow is proven.
wouldApplyIf: the arm is blocked or catching

commonConfusion.name: [S24] scaled jets = failed arm/pump
commonConfusion.note: Mineral scale in the tiny jet holes restricts flow and rotation - clean/descale the jets (per the manufacturer) first. A local one-arm/one-rack scale restriction is not the circulation pump or inlet valve.
wouldApplyIf: one arm or one rack washes poorly with visibly scaled jets

discriminators: Split the fault: ONE arm affected => that arm (blockage, split/damage, mounting/bearing) or a diverter where fitted. ALL spray weak => a common upstream cause (underfill/low water, restricted fill/matrix, or the circulation pump), not both arms failing independently.

A LEAK at the door during washing with a visibly SPLIT/CRACKED lower spray arm is caused by the arm firing water sideways at the door - raise the damaged spray arm as the source, not automatically the door seal.
Ticking/knocking/rattling in time with the wash is usually the arm catching a tall item or a loose/damaged arm, not a pump fault.

[S24] LOCAL vs SYSTEMIC: one arm / one rack / one group of jets favours a LOCAL spray-arm or distribution restriction; slow fill / low water level / ALL spray weak / whole machine washing poorly favours a COMMON water-delivery, level or circulation restriction. Don't diagnose several failed parts when one restricted water path fits better.

[S24] Mineral SCALE (as well as food debris) restricts spray-arm jets: reduced pressure, distorted pattern, poor rotation, one rack cleaning badly, progressively worse. UPPER arm jets scaled + top rack poor while the bottom rack is fine = a LOCAL upper spray-arm restriction, NOT the inlet valve, matrix or circulation pump. ALL spray weak points upstream (level/circulation), not the arms.

[S24] PROGRESSIVE vs SUDDEN: gradual worsening favours scale/restriction/contamination; a sudden failure (worked yesterday, dead/completely different today) favours a discrete blockage, failed component, electrical fault or leak - not scale. Not absolute.

rinse the jets/holes through
check the arm spins freely and isn't split, cracked or loose

Burning smell, scorched or exposed wiring, smoke, or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate at the socket/spur.

no salt added

the salt cap is loose

commonConfusion.name: [S24] adding salt fixes existing scale
commonConfusion.note: Salt and the correct hardness setting PREVENT scale and keep the softener working - they will NOT dissolve an existing heavy restriction. Separate correct operation (prevention) from repairing an existing scaled water path.
wouldApplyIf: there is already a heavy scale restriction

discriminators: [S24] The internal softener uses resin regenerated by dishwasher SALT; empty salt or a wrong hardness setting lets scale build up over time. This is mostly a CHECK/settings/maintenance matter (top up salt, set the hardness to the local supply) - only a genuinely faulty softener/sensor is a part. Adding salt PREVENTS future scale but does not clear an existing restriction.

[S24] Hard water is EVIDENCE, not proof: a hard-water area PLUS progressive water-path symptoms PLUS visible scale/restriction raises a scale/restriction cause - hard-water location ALONE is never a diagnosis.
adviceBeforeReplacement: top up dishwasher salt
set the water-hardness level to match your supply
run a manufacturer-approved descale/maintenance wash for existing film
dishwasher:conductivity-sensor.safety: SAFETY (authoritative): dishwashers run on mains electricity and hold water. Do NOT tell the customer to work on live wiring, open or move the door wiring loom while powered, perform live-voltage/continuity/insulation tests, bypass the RCD or earth, or repeatedly reset a machine that trips the electricity. Safe visible/mechanical checks with the machine switched off are fine. Follow only manufacturer-approved cleaning/descaling; do not scrape heating elements, sensors or plastics or mix cleaning chemicals. Burning smell, scorched or exposed wiring, smoke, or repeated tripping => STOP USE and isolate at the socket/spur.
dishwasher:conductivity-sensor.clarifyingQuestion: Is the salt light on or the hardness setting unset and the glasses going cloudy/chalky - or is there an actual water-path restriction?

likelyComponents: burner cap and ports seating / cleanliness
discriminators: Lights but won’t stay lit when you release the knob = the FSD/thermocouple.

likelyComponents: blocked pump filter / foreign object in the pump (clear first)
kinked or blocked drain hose / waste connection
drain pump (jammed impeller or failed motor)
discriminators: If the pump hums but little/no water leaves, the impeller is jammed or the filter/hose is blocked — clear those before condemning the pump.

commonConfusion.name: won't pump out = replace the drain pump
commonConfusion.note: A pump that hums or is noisy does NOT prove a failed pump. A blocked pump filter, a trapped foreign object, a kinked/blocked drain hose or a sump obstruction gives the same symptom - clear those first. Condemn the pump only once the filter, hose, sump and any foreign object are confirmed clear (see not-draining).
wouldApplyIf: filter, hose, sump and foreign objects all confirmed clear and the pump still hums with no flow, or is silent when drain is commanded

likelyComponents: drive motor (brushes / windings) — check the drum turns and motor runs
motor-control triac or relay on the main PCB
discriminators: Separate motor from board: a motor that never runs on any programme points at the motor or its triac/relay on the board.

commonConfusion.name: triac error code = the control board has failed
commonConfusion.note: A motor/heater triac code identifies the switching PATH, not a proven board failure. A motor that won't run can be the motor itself, its wiring/connector, or the triac/relay on the board - separate the motor from the board (does it never run on any programme?) before condemning the PCB.
wouldApplyIf: the motor never runs on any programme AND the motor, its wiring and connector are proven good

likelyComponents: mechanical jam / foreign object / seizing bearing (turn the drum by hand first)
discriminators: An over-current cut-out is usually a mechanical jam or a failing motor — check the drum spins freely by hand before parts.

commonConfusion.name: over-current code = a failed motor
commonConfusion.note: An over-current / motor-overload trip is USUALLY a mechanical jam or drag (a trapped foreign object, a seizing bearing, an obstruction) rather than a failed motor. Check the drum turns freely by hand with the power off and clear any obstruction before condemning the motor or its control.
wouldApplyIf: the drum turns freely by hand with no obstruction and the over-current trip still persists

likelyComponents: water supply / inlet filter / fill path (check first)
discriminators: A flow-meter fault looks like slow/short fill — rule out the tap, hose and inlet filter first.

commonConfusion.name: fill / flow error code = replace the flow meter
commonConfusion.note: A flow-meter / fill code reports slow or short fill, which is far more often the water supply (tap part-off, low pressure), a kinked fill hose or a blocked inlet mesh filter than the flow sensor itself. Rule out the tap, hose and inlet filter before the flow meter.
wouldApplyIf: tap fully on, hose unkinked and inlet filter clean, yet fill is still slow/short

discriminators: Rule out a genuinely unbalanced load and poor levelling before the vibration sensor.

commonConfusion.name: vibration-sensor code = replace the sensor
commonConfusion.note: A MEMS / vibration-sensor code (or a repeated spin-abort) is usually a genuinely unbalanced load or poor levelling rather than a failed sensor. Rule out load distribution, overloading and levelling/feet before the vibration sensor.
wouldApplyIf: load balanced and redistributed, machine level and not overloaded, yet the sensor fault / spin-abort still persists

likelyComponents: blocked pump filter / foreign object (clear first)
kinked / blocked drain hose or waste connection
discriminators: Won’t drain and won’t spin is almost always the pump or a blocked filter — it won’t spin until it has drained.
Slow or no fill: check the tap, hose and inlet filter before the valve.

likelyComponents: retained water / cycle not finished (lock correctly held)
discriminators: A door stuck locked after an interrupted cycle is usually a drain/heater fault leaving it mid-programme, not a failed lock.
No heat on a hot wash: element or NTC — confirm it really filled and a hot programme was set first.

likelyComponents: clean the lint filter / condenser (film insulates the sensor)
discriminators: Poor auto-dry is often a filmed sensor or blocked condenser — clean first.

likelyComponents: clean the condenser / lint filter and clear the airflow
discriminators: Over-temperature on drying is usually airflow (filter/condenser/fan) before an electrical part.

likelyComponents: rule out the direct causes first (supply, door, heater, motor, pump)
control PCB (power section for a dead machine)
blocked pump filter / foreign object (clear first)
drain hose / waste kink or blockage
discriminators: Hums but doesn’t pump = jammed impeller or blocked filter/hose; clear before replacing the pump.

likelyComponents: pressure chamber / sensing hose (blocked or split)
motor-control triac / relay on the board
water supply / inlet filter / fill path first
drum bearing (if the real complaint is noise/play)
property socket / supply / fused spur (test with another appliance)
discriminators: Completely dead: prove the socket and plug fuse before internal parts.

likelyComponents: wiring between the UI and main board

discriminators: Violent movement on spin: first rule out transit bolts and a bad load, then dampers/springs, then bearings.

likelyComponents: wash heater element leaking to earth
drying heater element leaking to earth
drain / wash pump leaking to earth
symptoms: trips as soon as i turn it on
trips when it starts to heat
trips after it has been drying a while
discriminators: WHEN it trips localises the earth fault by PHASE (a washer-dryer has two heaters). Trips the instant it is switched on / as it fills = wiring/short, a shorted pump, the mains lead or the suppressor. Trips once the WASH water starts HEATING = the WASH heater element leaking to earth. Trips when the DRYING phase starts to heat = the DRYING heater element (or its wiring) leaking to earth. Water getting into wiring/connectors can trip it at any point.
Isolate by timing: which part of the cycle trips it (power-up, fill, wash-heat, spin, or when drying heats)? That points to wiring/pump vs the wash heater vs the drying heater.
adviceBeforeReplacement: do NOT keep resetting the RCD/breaker and re-running an appliance that repeatedly trips the supply - stop use where there is a credible electrical fault
note the timing of the trip (on power / on fill / when the wash heats / on spin / when drying heats) to localise the fault before replacing a part
washer-dryer:tripping-electrics.safety: ADVISORY ONLY (deterministic safety remains authoritative): an appliance that repeatedly trips the electrics should be taken out of use - do not repeatedly reset the breaker to keep testing it. Do not open the casing or test/probe live electrical parts.

safetyInformation.hazard: Dangerous wiring or an insulation fault (repeated tripping, a burning smell or scorch marks); water present raises shock risk, and a washer-dryer has a hot drying heater as well as the wash heater.
safetyInformation.applicability: Appliance repeatedly trips the electrics, or there is a burning smell / scorching.
